pairs.tendency: In the print and play game Stop the Spread, students run a paper simulation of viral spread with dice, choose an intervention, run it again and compare the two results.
pros: Students can follow cause and effect and put their attention on collecting and graphing data.

source.ref: and Ford Morgan, H. (None). Not by chance: Developing tabletop games to increase awareness of data science. . https://doi.org/10.5204/thesis.eprints.239445 (Pages cited are those of the open-access PDF.)

pairs.tendency: In Virtual Reef Diver: Tabletop Edition a point is earned for each organism correctly categorised, and players can use what has already been revealed to work out what a card is likely to be.
pros: Remembering and predicting leads to more points, which encourages simple analysis of the cards on the table.

source.ref: and Ford Morgan, H. (None). Not by chance: Developing tabletop games to increase awareness of data science. . https://doi.org/10.5204/thesis.eprints.239445 (Pages cited are those of the open-access PDF.)

pairs.tendency: Players swap resources with each other so that one of them can complete a set.
pros: Trading lets a player complete a set, and players talk to each other to do it.

pairs.tendency: Bidding is often run together with trading, so the value of what a player adds to a deal changes with the bids.

pairs.tendency: Hand management and set collection tend to be paired in educational games and support each other in passing on information.

pairs.tendency: Tile placement is often combined with area majority, and each tile turned over scores a victory point for the player who opens it.
pros: Tile placement is one of the easiest mechanics to learn.

source.ref: Acar, A. P. and Güler, T. (2025). Board Game Design As Alternative Educational Material and Frequently Used Game Mechanics. Dokuz Eylül Üniversitesi Buca Eğitim Fakültesi Dergisi, 1367–1398. https://doi.org/10.53444/deubefd.1463581

pairs.tendency: When each player's letters are hidden, players work out what the other holds from what was played, and a play can be made to push the opponent into a wrong guess.
pros: A play that threatens a word you cannot make can make the opponent block it, and the paper shows that mixing such bluffs in at random can be the sound play even against an opponent who reasons perfectly.
Reading the opponent's unseen tiles from their earlier plays gives bluffing something to work on.
cons: The paper expects this kind of bluff to pay in few positions, and only where the circumstances are just right.

source.ref: Ballard, N. and Chow, T. Y. (2025). Bluffing in Scrabble. arXiv preprint, not peer reviewed. https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2509.10471 (Pages cited are those of the open-access PDF.)

pairs.tendency: When cards are dealt at random but each hand stays hidden, luck sets the start and players then keep updating what they believe the other hand holds, so experience tends to pay off.
pros: Players with more experience tend to win more often
Hidden hands give play a belief-updating element that rewards skill
cons: The deal itself is left to chance

source.ref: Banerjee, T., De, A., Maitra, S. and Mukherjee, D. (2024). Skill vs. Chance Quantification for Popular Card & Board Games. arXiv preprint, not peer reviewed. https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2410.14363 (Pages cited are those of the open-access PDF.)

pairs.tendency: A dice roll decides which moves are open on each turn, but choosing well among them still makes a measurable difference.
pros: Smart strategy gives an edge over players who lack it
cons: The roll dictates the choices on offer each turn

source.ref: Banerjee, T., De, A., Maitra, S. and Mukherjee, D. (2024). Skill vs. Chance Quantification for Popular Card & Board Games. arXiv preprint, not peer reviewed. https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2410.14363 (Pages cited are those of the open-access PDF.)

pairs.tendency: When players bet on cards nobody else can see, repeated play can reward judging odds and bluffing, though a single round is mostly decided by chance.
pros: Repeated play may reward probabilistic thinking
Bluffing skill can pay off over many rounds
cons: Short-term results are heavily driven by chance because other players' cards cannot be seen
Little room for strategic depth within one round

source.ref: Banerjee, T., De, A., Maitra, S. and Mukherjee, D. (2024). Skill vs. Chance Quantification for Popular Card & Board Games. arXiv preprint, not peer reviewed. https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2410.14363 (Pages cited are those of the open-access PDF.)

pairs.tendency: In a partner race, one player may hold back to block or hit rivals, so a lead for one partner is not the end.
pros: A player can move a partner's piece instead of their own
Holding back lets one partner shield the other
cons: A partner who rushes out of the game leaves the other facing two throws for one
Opponents can keep just behind a lone partner and send him back with a capture

pairs.tendency: When partners take turns in a fixed order, a team that loses one player leaves the other with one turn against two.
pros: The remaining partner keeps playing
Partners can cover each other's pieces
cons: The lone partner is hit again and again by two sets of throws
A team can lose by one player finishing early

source.ref: Bell, R. C. (1960). Board and table games from many civilizations. London: Oxford University Press. (The copy read is this first volume; the Dover one-volume revised edition of 1979, ISBN 978-0-486-23855-5, keeps its page numbers.)

pairs.tendency: When some throws give another turn, one player can move several times in a row while the others wait.
pros: A player who throws a five or a four and has a second throw may split the two throws across two horses
The extra throw ends only on a low score, so the run has an edge
cons: A capture also earns the capturer an extra turn
One long run can decide a short game

source.ref: Bell, R. C. (1960). Board and table games from many civilizations. London: Oxford University Press. (The copy read is this first volume; the Dover one-volume revised edition of 1979, ISBN 978-0-486-23855-5, keeps its page numbers.)

pairs.tendency: A throw that can be split or added softens luck, but a rule to play every number can still force a costly move.
pros: The numbers can be shared between pieces
The player picks which piece takes each number
cons: Playing the whole throw is required if any move exists
One throw can break up pairs and leave single pieces open to a hit

source.ref: Bell, R. C. (1960). Board and table games from many civilizations. London: Oxford University Press. (The copy read is this first volume; the Dover one-volume revised edition of 1979, ISBN 978-0-486-23855-5, keeps its page numbers.)

pairs.tendency: With safe squares, only a piece in the open can be hit, so players choose when to wait and when to run.
pros: A piece on a safe square cannot be sent back
A hit sends a piece to the start and may bring another throw
cons: A piece resting in the last castle waits there until a twenty-five is thrown
A castle held by one player's piece is closed to enemy pieces

pairs.tendency: Dice were played for money, and to prevent cheating they were thrown through a straw ring in Nyout and into a spiral tower in Rome.
pros: Nero is said to have played for as much as 400,000 sesterces on a point
Korean lower classes play Nyout for money in public houses
cons: Money on the dice invites cheating, so the dice are thrown through a ring or down a tower
In later Rome gambling grew into a mania

source.ref: Bell, R. C. (1960). Board and table games from many civilizations. London: Oxford University Press. (The copy read is this first volume; the Dover one-volume revised edition of 1979, ISBN 978-0-486-23855-5, keeps its page numbers.)

pairs.tendency: Where dice and money were banned together, Shaturanga players took the die out and left only skill.
pros: Dropping the die removed the element of luck
Taking out the dice gave a way round the law
cons: Hindu law punished the gambler and the host of the gambling house
A ban on stakes can change how a game is played

source.ref: Bell, R. C. (1960). Board and table games from many civilizations. London: Oxford University Press. (The copy read is this first volume; the Dover one-volume revised edition of 1979, ISBN 978-0-486-23855-5, keeps its page numbers.)

pairs.tendency: In the Hyena Game the first player home gets a hyena that hunts the other mothers, so winning the race starts a chase.
pros: The winner has something to do against rivals
Players still on the track stay in play
cons: A mother that is eaten loses by more than one that gets home safe
On leaving the well the hyena keeps double speed and overtaken mothers are eaten

source.ref: Bell, R. C. (1960). Board and table games from many civilizations. London: Oxford University Press. (The copy read is this first volume; the Dover one-volume revised edition of 1979, ISBN 978-0-486-23855-5, keeps its page numbers.)

pairs.tendency: A dice walk can be a journey from a village to a well and back, with saved scores paying for the trip.
pros: Each space reads as a day's walk
Scores saved as tokens pay for washing, a drink and the hyena's release
cons: A score that does not move the piece can leave a player standing still
A mother short of tabas at the well waits until her son has collected them

source.ref: Bell, R. C. (1960). Board and table games from many civilizations. London: Oxford University Press. (The copy read is this first volume; the Dover one-volume revised edition of 1979, ISBN 978-0-486-23855-5, keeps its page numbers.)

pairs.tendency: A dice walk can be scored in counters won and lost at a river, a meeting or a lap.
pros: Every lap, meeting or fall in the water moves a counter
The game can end early if one side holds every counter
cons: A runner who falls into a dry river bed costs the team a throw
A time limit decides the winner by a count at that moment

source.ref: Bell, R. C. (1960). Board and table games from many civilizations. London: Oxford University Press. (The copy read is this first volume; the Dover one-volume revised edition of 1979, ISBN 978-0-486-23855-5, keeps its page numbers.)

pairs.tendency: Copies of the Goose plan were made to teach history and geography, with a fact placed on each space.
pros: The Goose idea was reused for lessons in history, geography, buildings, plants and the stars
Later copies were coloured by hand and mounted on canvas
cons: Each throw is added to the counter's place, so the dice fix where it lands
A player may pass over some spaces without learning them

pairs.tendency: In the drinking form of Sixe-Ace, the last player or two on the board pay for the drinks.
pros: Most players are safe once their side is clear
Throws of one pass a piece on, so trouble moves round the table
cons: A throw of two means a drink and another throw
The dice decide who pays

pairs.tendency: In Go, the winner is whoever holds more points in the end, so a loss in one corner can be paid back in another.
pros: A setback in one part of the board does not end the game
A group that cannot be saved can be left while play turns elsewhere
cons: The finer points of play cannot be set out in a few pages
A full game usually lasts about an hour and may last three

source.ref: Bell, R. C. (1960). Board and table games from many civilizations. London: Oxford University Press. (The copy read is this first volume; the Dover one-volume revised edition of 1979, ISBN 978-0-486-23855-5, keeps its page numbers.)

pairs.tendency: When skill decides who holds more ground, a player who keeps winning can start with fewer stones so that the other player has a close game.
pros: Players of different strength can still meet on even terms
A run of wins changes the start of the next game
cons: A player who receives a handicap plays Black and moves second
If the stronger player keeps winning, the handicap grows step by step

source.ref: Bell, R. C. (1960). Board and table games from many civilizations. London: Oxford University Press. (The copy read is this first volume; the Dover one-volume revised edition of 1979, ISBN 978-0-486-23855-5, keeps its page numbers.)

pairs.tendency: When pieces are first placed and then moved to make lines, the placing can decide how the moving part goes.
pros: A line of three pieces lets the player take one of the other's pieces
Both players place twelve pieces one at a time, in turn
cons: A line of four pieces does not count
Play stops once a player can form no further lines of three

source.ref: Bell, R. C. (1960). Board and table games from many civilizations. London: Oxford University Press. (The copy read is this first volume; the Dover one-volume revised edition of 1979, ISBN 978-0-486-23855-5, keeps its page numbers.)

pairs.tendency: In Seega everything is visible and a piece is taken only between two enemy pieces, so a player can wall in their own pieces where nothing can reach them.
pros: Careful players can build a group that is safe
The placing phase sets up much of the fight
cons: The game can end in a draw or on a count of pieces
A player who cannot move leaves the other to open a way by taking an extra turn

source.ref: Bell, R. C. (1960). Board and table games from many civilizations. London: Oxford University Press. (The copy read is this first volume; the Dover one-volume revised edition of 1979, ISBN 978-0-486-23855-5, keeps its page numbers.)

pairs.tendency: When dice or coins decide and real money or goods are on the table, the stakes are what draw people to the game.
pros: Large sums changed hands at Hazard
Players also made side bets among themselves, and the book gives odds for them from an 1786 Hoyle
cons: Players can lose far more than the game itself is worth
Without the stakes, little is left to keep people playing

source.ref: Bell, R. C. (1960). Board and table games from many civilizations. London: Oxford University Press. (The copy read is this first volume; the Dover one-volume revised edition of 1979, ISBN 978-0-486-23855-5, keeps its page numbers.)

pairs.tendency: Awari is a game of skill, and among the Saramacca people it is played in a house of mourning to keep the dead company.
pros: Awari is treated as a mind game of the rank of chess
People play for a reason other than winning
cons: The game stops at dusk, when ghosts are thought to join in
Playing is tied to rules from outside, such as who may make the board

source.ref: Bell, R. C. (1960). Board and table games from many civilizations. London: Oxford University Press. (The copy read is this first volume; the Dover one-volume revised edition of 1979, ISBN 978-0-486-23855-5, keeps its page numbers.)

pairs.tendency: In Liar Dice, a false claim or a wrong challenge costs a life, so players are worn down one by one.
pros: A fourth life is granted to whoever first uses up three, a grace called being on the parish
There is a clear last player at the end
cons: One wrong guess costs only a single life, so a player stays in after a mistake
A player who loses all three lives is out of the game

source.ref: Bell, R. C. (1960). Board and table games from many civilizations. London: Oxford University Press. (The copy read is this first volume; the Dover one-volume revised edition of 1979, ISBN 978-0-486-23855-5, keeps its page numbers.)

pairs.tendency: In Bell and Hammer, cards are bought at an auction, and later the dice decide who pays and who is paid.
pros: The five picture cards are sold one at a time to the successful bidders
The card a player owns decides how each throw affects them
cons: Once the auction is over, the dice settle almost everything
A player who is out of two successive rounds leaves the game and the counters go to the pool

source.ref: Bell, R. C. (1960). Board and table games from many civilizations. London: Oxford University Press. (The copy read is this first volume; the Dover one-volume revised edition of 1979, ISBN 978-0-486-23855-5, keeps its page numbers.)

pairs.tendency: In Forty-Two, each player bids once, and the bid sets the number of points the bidding side promises to win in the tricks.
pros: The highest bidder leads and names the trump suit
Each player gets one bid, and every bid has to beat the one before
cons: One bid each keeps the bidding short
If the bid is not made, the opponents score the bid together with their own points

source.ref: Bell, R. C. (1960). Board and table games from many civilizations. London: Oxford University Press. (The copy read is this first volume; the Dover one-volume revised edition of 1979, ISBN 978-0-486-23855-5, keeps its page numbers.)

pairs.tendency: In the domino game Bingo, a trick winner may stop the drawing and promise 70 points, winning more if it works and giving the other player more if not.
pros: A turn holds a choice between waiting and committing
A lead can be turned into a bigger win
cons: A failed promise gives the other player double
Once drawing has stopped, the other player has to answer in the suit led or with a trump

source.ref: Bell, R. C. (1960). Board and table games from many civilizations. London: Oxford University Press. (The copy read is this first volume; the Dover one-volume revised edition of 1979, ISBN 978-0-486-23855-5, keeps its page numbers.)

pairs.tendency: In Domino Crib, each player gives away two of six tiles before play, so the hand is kept for the sums, pairs and runs it can make.
pros: The crib is counted for the dealer together with the starter tile
Counting fifteens, pairs and runs gives many small scores
cons: The tiles given away go to the dealer's crib, so they help the dealer
The opponent of the dealer counts first, which can decide a close game

source.ref: Bell, R. C. (1960). Board and table games from many civilizations. London: Oxford University Press. (The copy read is this first volume; the Dover one-volume revised edition of 1979, ISBN 978-0-486-23855-5, keeps its page numbers.)

pairs.tendency: In Ma-jong, a player may keep a set of four tiles hidden so that the others cannot tell which suit is being collected.
pros: Hiding a set also hides the plan
A hidden set scores more than the same set shown
cons: A concealed set not yet put down counts only as a pung and an odd tile if another player goes out
A player cannot go out until a loose tile has been drawn to make up for the fourth tile of a four set

source.ref: Bell, R. C. (1960). Board and table games from many civilizations. London: Oxford University Press. (The copy read is this first volume; the Dover one-volume revised edition of 1979, ISBN 978-0-486-23855-5, keeps its page numbers.)

pairs.tendency: In Ma-jong, any player may claim the last discarded tile out of turn to finish a set, and the players passed over lose their turn.
pros: A player holding two tiles like the last discard can call pung and take it
Only the next player in turn can chow a discard
cons: The tile can be claimed only until the next discard
The order of play is uneven, because a call can skip players

pros: Each player starts by putting the same number of counters into the pool
Everyone can see the pool grow and shrink
cons: After the first stake, players make no choices
A player who has lost all counters retires from the game

Each turn is short
cons: Players only compare totals at the end

pairs.tendency: In the Block game, players hold their tiles out of sight and lose their turn when no tile matches an open end.

In a blocked game the lowest count scores the spots in the other hands as well as its own
cons: A player with no matching tile misses turns until an end changes
The tiles a player is dealt limit the moves open to them

A player with few matching tiles draws from the pile and may still pass

pairs.tendency: When the last seed of every sowing has to land in one store, with falling short or going past losing the game, the starting layout alone settles whether a win is possible and which moves win.
cons: The game can be unwinnable from the first layout, and a winnable one leaves a single series of moves.

pairs.tendency: In a dice race with snakes and ladders, which squares carry them changes how long a game lasts, and a short ladder can matter more than a long one.
pros: A short ladder on the right square can shorten the game a lot.

pairs.tendency: When the special squares are named virtues and vices, moving along the board reads as a path of virtuous and wicked actions, as in Gyan Chaupar.
pros: Climbing a ladder or sliding down a snake carries a meaning players can read straight from the board.

pairs.tendency: In Chowka Bhara a piece landed on by an opponent goes back to its start, except on the marked safe squares, which also let any number of pieces share one square.
pros: A piece on a safe square cannot be hit, and pieces of different players can sit together there.

pairs.tendency: In Chowka Bhara a player who hits an opponent's piece is paid with a bonus throw, so hitting leads straight into more movement.
pros: A hit gives another throw in the same turn.

pairs.tendency: In Chowka Bhara a throw of 4 or 8 on the cowry shells brings a bonus throw, and the values from one turn can be split between pieces.
pros: A bonus throw lets a player move one piece several times or spread the moves over different pieces.
cons: A third 4 or 8 in a row means no move at all and the turn passes.

pairs.tendency: In Chowka Bhara a piece needs an exact throw to reach the finishing square, so throws that are too large cannot be used by that piece.
cons: A throw larger than the squares left cannot move that piece, and a player with only that piece left loses the turn.

pairs.tendency: Sowing games are only holes and counters, so different communities have given them their own meanings, such as sown seeds, fish-shaped boards, or counters called cows in a trade theme
pros: Many local meanings can be projected onto the same set of holes and counters

pros: Players do not have to build their decks at the same time or together

pairs.tendency: Roll and move is familiar to learners and is often used to deliver quiz questions, but on its own it usually adds nothing beyond that.
pros: learners already understand the mechanic
cons: it does not usually add value in itself

pairs.tendency: When players are knocked out one by one and play goes round the table, the players who are out sit and wait while the rest finish.
pros: A knocked-out player is not made to play on with no hope.
Players who are out can fetch a snack or take a short rest.
cons: Players who are out may wander off before the next game starts.
A long game after the first knock-out can break up the session.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When every player can see how far everyone has got, a player far behind can tell early that they cannot win the race.
pros: Nobody has to guess who leads.
A rule that lets one turn gain any distance keeps every player in the running.
cons: A player behind may stay seated with no chance of winning.
One huge turn can end the game on its first round.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When players build their own scores side by side, the winner is the highest total, and players seldom change each other's totals.
pros: Players behind can still try to raise their own score.
Races have little interactivity, so more players can be added until physical limits stop them.
cons: A player far behind can see early that they cannot win.
A player out of the running has little way to affect the others.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: With no rival at the table, shuffles and dice supply the surprise, so a team plays against the cards or the dice.
pros: The designer can set how often the team wins, such as about seven games in ten.
A team on one side is the team version of a single-player game.
cons: Players who learn the pattern of the deck can use up its surprise.
A team that wins every time tends to lose interest.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When players lay tiles on a shared board, a tile can block a rival or set up your own next move, and this pays less as more players join.
pros: With two players, blocking the board hurts the one rival.
Setting up your next move is worth the effort.
cons: With more players, setting up a position or damaging a rival pays less while its cost stays the same.
Where the payoff falls far enough, strong players may drop these moves from the strategies they use.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: A team game can be played with no fixed sides by giving one point to each member of the winning team and mixing the teams every round.
pros: Everyone has a score of their own.
A large group can play without fixed sides.
cons: Players who like keeping the same teammates tend to turn it down.
The final winner can feel far from any one round.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When a player is beaten but a hidden part of the map is left, that player can hide there and delay the end.
pros: A hidden map gives a losing player something to try.
A rule that shows the hidden pieces of a player with no army ends the game soon after.
cons: Finding the last hidden piece can take a long time.
The winner may wait with nothing to do.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: A game with short rounds can be played in a street or park for as long as people have, so passers-by can join and leave.
pros: Players fit a game into a lunch break or recess.
Short rounds suit a game whose length no one knows in advance.
cons: It needs enough people to turn up.
More rounds in the same time mean more pauses between rounds.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: A role-playing game with no winner and no ending has no clear game, only evenings of play and a long campaign that links them.
pros: Paper role-playing games are rarely completed in one session, so play carries on across sessions.
The same story and characters can run for months.
cons: Nobody can say who did well.
The rules give no ending condition to mark the finish.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When one side is far ahead in a thinking game played until one side is gone, the losing player may not see the game is lost.
pros: Chess has developed customs of resignation that deal with hopeless positions.
A player who sees the loss early can end the game and start another.
cons: A beginner may not know the position is lost.
A stubborn player can keep a hopeless game going.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When the score is money or chips kept after the game, a player with no chance of winning still cares how the last hands turn out.
pros: A player behind still has a reason to play carefully.
Players keep a record from game to game.
cons: Players with no chance may just play for a small gain.
Chasing money can pull attention from beating the others.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: A rule that lets the player who is ahead offer to double the stake rewards players who read the position correctly.
pros: The player who judges the position more closely is paid for it.
A player who accepts a doubled stake wrongly pays for it.
cons: The rule only works if players play for points or money.
A player with weak positional judgement may not see that they are losing.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: With three or more players who can pick any target, players tend to gang up on whoever looks closest to winning.
pros: The lead changes hands many times.
Players who are behind keep a chance until late.
cons: Skill at the game's own moves matters less than steering others towards someone else.
The player furthest ahead is often the first to be knocked out.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When players can hurt any rival they choose, talk fills the table: pleas, threats, promises of revenge and offers from outside the game.
pros: Players enjoy the give and take, and onlookers can follow it.
Few game rules are needed, because the talk carries the game.
cons: Arguments start over why one player was picked.
Detailed rules and charts get lost under the deal-making.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Points give a player who cannot win something to aim at, so the group has fewer reasons to pick on one leader.
pros: Players out of the running still have a reason to play carefully.
Players spend less effort ganging up on the leader.
cons: Players may disagree on whether to chase first place or the highest score.
A player far behind may stop caring about winning outright.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When the aim is to avoid losing, players tend to pick on whoever is behind.
pros: Most players are safe once someone is knocked out.
The game can stop as soon as one player drops out.
cons: The player who is behind becomes the target.
A slow start is hard to recover from.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: If you can only attack the players your pieces touch, the choice of victim comes from the map, not from taste.
pros: Attacks have a reason: the neighbour holds something you want.
Players are less likely to feel picked on for no reason.
cons: Players far from each other never meet.
A player may hang back and let neighbours fight.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: If play lasts until one army is gone, players often hold back and wait for others to weaken each other.
pros: A single clear winner is left at the end.
Fights decide who survives.
cons: Players who hang back can slow the whole game down.
Early losers wait a long time while the others finish.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: A pure race lets players barely touch each other, so any number can join and the game never needs a victim.
pros: More players can be added up to the limits of the table.
Nobody can decide the winner by a choice made out of pity or spite.
cons: Even where players cannot affect each other, they often react to each other's progress and change how they play.
With only two players, there is little reason to play against someone.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: In a race, players tend to play safe when ahead and take bigger risks when behind.
pros: A player who is behind can take bigger risks in an effort to win.
The leader has to choose how much to risk.
cons: A player who is behind and takes a risk may fall even further behind.
Players in front and behind play in different ways.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Blocking squares or sending pieces back lets players affect a race without choosing a person to hurt.
pros: Players in a race can still affect each other, for example by blockading or sending pieces home.
In many European boardgames, a player's actions change which point-gathering strategies stay open to others.
cons: The more players can block, the less the game feels like a plain race.
Some of the picking-on-the-leader behaviour comes back.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When your actions change which scoring routes are open to others, players affect each other without anyone being chosen as a target.
pros: Players still affect one another, because a player's actions change which scoring strategies stay open.
Players in a lost position can aim for something more definite.
cons: A player out of the running can still decide who wins.
Players need to read the board to know who is ahead.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Moving first helps most when two players are evenly matched; at lower skill the advantage tends to fade.
pros: Beginners are hardly affected by who goes first.
Swapping who starts, or playing several games, evens things out.
cons: Two experts can find the first mover keeps an edge.
One game alone cannot cancel the edge.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: A rule that forces a move after a set time can leave players using all of that time, so games can run longer.
pros: Turns cannot go on for ever.
The rule is meant to speed up play.
cons: Players tend to use the full allowed time.
The average game can take longer than before.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When all players choose at the same moment from the same options, nobody has a seat or turn position that helps more.
pros: No one gains from going first.
Everyone starts on equal terms.
cons: Games where everyone moves at once from the same options are rare.
A time trial is symmetric only while riders do not know how others have done.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Splitting many players into two sides removes the choice of whom to attack, since the opponents are already named.
pros: A large group can play without anyone being picked on.
No player is left deciding the winner from outside the contest.
cons: A teammate's slip can cost the whole side.
Players feel angry when a teammate makes a mistake.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Cards that a partner cannot see stop a stronger partner from telling the other exactly what to play.
pros: Hidden information leaves an expert without enough knowledge to direct a beginner.
Signals between partners become part of the play.
cons: Partners cannot tell each other what they hold.
Rules have to stop players from simply telling teammates what they hold.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: In partner card games, direct talk is forbidden, so partners send signals through their bids and the cards they play.
pros: Reading a partner's signals becomes much of the interest.
Neither partner can play the other's hand.
cons: A partner's slip costs both of you.
Once one hand is laid open, no signals pass at all.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Bids work as messages to a partner, and the same bid can mean different things from different seats.
pros: Bidding carries information without breaking the no-talking rule.
Players learn a shared system of meanings.
cons: Partners need to agree the meanings before they play.
A bid read the wrong way can mislead a partner.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When everyone sees everything and no clock runs, the strongest player tends to tell the others what to play.
pros: Modest amounts of advice from an experienced player can help teammates.
Everyone can follow the plan.
cons: A beginner can be left with nothing to decide.
Players may argue over who is allowed to give orders.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Cards that only their holder can see stop one expert from running the whole team.
pros: Each player's knowledge is theirs alone.
Players need ways to share without simply telling.
cons: Players have to hold back what they know.
The team may waste moves from missing information.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: A clock leaves no time for one player to give every instruction, so each person still has to act for themselves.
pros: Each player's moves matter.
Where speed is needed an experienced player can advise, yet what the other players do still counts.
cons: Hurried players make mistakes that fall on teammates.
Beginners may feel pushed.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Skill in the hands cannot be handed over by instruction, so telling a teammate what to do still leaves the doing to them.
pros: Each player's own hands count.
Advice from a stronger player helps without taking over.
cons: A less experienced player may be unable to carry out the advice they are given.
Players can feel let down when a teammate drops something.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When talk is not allowed, nobody can order a teammate, and meaning has to travel by what is played.
pros: No one can take over another's role.
In bridge, much of the interest lies in how partners signal within the limits on talk.
cons: Partners cannot simply tell each other what they hold.
The team cannot fix a plan with a quick word.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Playing a character gives a player a reason to turn down a teammate's orders, because it is in character to do so.
pros: Advice can be refused without an argument.
Each character brings its own part to the team.
cons: Less experienced players may not follow advice, since some prefer to go their own way.
The strongest player may still push their view.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When points stand for money or something else that counts, players keep playing for points even when they cannot win.
pros: Players who cannot win still have a reason to play.
Players have less urge to throw the game to a rival.
cons: Players have little reason to chase points that are worth nothing.
Players ahead and behind may want different things from one game.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Keeping money for spending apart from points for winning gives a player who is behind on points a way to catch up.
pros: Players behind can recover.
The game seems close until the end.
cons: A second track adds more to learn.
Players weigh a quick lead against saving money for later.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: With no formal winner, groups choose their own aim, such as keeping a Hacky Sack in the air as long as possible.
pros: The group picks an aim that suits it.
Players can find the game satisfying in different ways.
cons: Players may pick different aims at the same table.
Nobody can say for certain who won.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When moves depend on a roll, a big lead tells you less than it seems, as one roll can change the order.
pros: Players far behind keep some hope of catching up.
A roll that moves every player forward is likely to help the one who is behind.
cons: Who is winning is hard to read from the board.
Choices made before a roll change the result very little.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: In a race you cannot spend your lead on anything else, so being ahead does not help the leader move faster.
pros: The lead does not feed on itself.
The lead works as an intuitive kind of victory point.
cons: Without a catch-up rule, the lead stays where the rolls put it.
Real races sometimes slow the leader, but a plain dice race does not.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When money from a lucky roll buys more power and the game ends by knock-out, the leader tends to pull further ahead.
pros: Players with no chance can leave sooner than in a game that drags on.
A snowball effect that leads straight to a finish can be a welcome thing.
cons: An early lead tends to settle the whole game.
Players who are knocked out wait for the others to finish.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When luck is part of the result, a leader gains by knocking out a trailing player before a lucky turn can rescue them.
pros: Leaders have a clear reason to press an advantage.
Games shorten, so nobody sits through a long hopeless stretch.
cons: A player behind gets no time to wait for a lucky turn.
Players near the bottom become targets.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Attacks that sometimes hit and sometimes miss keep the lead changing hands, as with missiles in a kart race.
pros: Players behind keep a way to catch up.
Hit-or-miss events make the lead change more often and most players find games livelier.
cons: The score or position says little about who is truly ahead.
Pushed far enough, players stop caring who leads.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When players can agree to act together, a clear leader tends to face everyone else, so a lead is hard to keep.
pros: Players behind stay in the game for a long time.
The lead changes hands often.
cons: Points gained early matter little to the result.
Players may aim for second place and jump ahead at the end.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: A random event moving everyone helps the player in last place and hurts the one in first, though on paper it treats all alike.
pros: Players behind keep hope.
A card sending everyone back to Start is welcome to a player who is losing a race.
cons: One turn can wipe out the leader's progress.
Players ahead may feel earlier moves were wasted.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Where luck is part of the result, players tend to take bigger risks when behind and safer lines when ahead.
pros: A player behind has a plan to try.
A player ahead has to choose how much to risk.
cons: Players ahead and behind end up playing different games.
With much randomness, the score may overstate how far ahead a leader really is.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: With nothing hidden and no dice, the number of legal moves decides how the game feels to play.
pros: Players who learn opening patterns have fewer moves to weigh.
Players can narrow many options by spotting duplicate moves and weak ones.
cons: A beginner facing very many moves ends up choosing almost at random.
A game with one clear right move stops feeling like a game.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: In Monopoly the number of real decisions starts low, grows once trading begins, and falls again when rolls decide who pays whom.
pros: The game has a shape like a story, with an opening, a middle and an end.
A rising and then falling number of choices gives the game its pacing.
cons: Early turns offer few decisions.
Late turns mostly wait on the dice.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Secret choices made together add uncertainty without any dice, so a skilful player can still lose to a lucky guess.
pros: Players who dislike dice often accept it, because it comes from choices.
Reading your opponents becomes part of the skill.
cons: Players with more expertise often dislike chance in a game, since it costs them wins.
A result can turn on a single guess.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Luck placed at the start, as in a deal, tends to be accepted more easily than luck that arrives after a plan is made.
pros: Players enjoy working out how to play the cards they hold.
The luck comes before the thinking, so a plan is not undone afterwards.
cons: An unlucky deal can make the game feel settled early.
Players may blame the deal for a loss.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: In paper role-play a key roll draws every eye, and as there are many rolls, one failure rarely ends the story.
pros: Players watch each roll with interest.
A failed plan can be replaced by a new one.
cons: Much can hang on a single roll.
Players may feel chance outweighs their planning.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: A map that is new each game throws up odd situations, so players cannot lean on memorised patterns.
pros: Each play differs, so players have reason to return.
Players learn general ways of thinking instead of fixed openings.
cons: Players with more expertise often dislike chance in a game, since it costs them wins.
Planning ahead is harder when the layout is unknown.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When players pick from a pool, one option far more powerful than the rest leaves a single sensible pick.
pros: A small pool in front of you keeps most options worth a look.
Players who study the pool can learn which picks matter.
cons: One very powerful option leaves nothing to choose.
The designer has to keep adjusting how powerful each option is.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When players leave the game as they finish and the last one left loses, each finisher is safe and drops out of the game.
pros: Players who are safe can relax or watch.
Snowball effects like these can help when a game drags on or elimination causes trouble.
cons: The player in trouble has to keep playing a game they expect to lose.
Nobody who has finished has reason to help the last player.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When each player secretly splits forces between areas at the same moment, no split is safe and guessing the other split decides the result.
pros: The same split of forces turns up in many military games with several important areas.
The same model covers how points are spread when designing a character or unit.
cons: Putting everything in one area ends the guessing.
Results can feel like a coin flip.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When some facts are known to one player only, each player plays from a different picture. Guessing and pretending join the game.
pros: Players get surprise and a feeling of discovery as things are shown.
The game becomes a contest of bluffing and insight as well as of moves.
cons: Players spend effort remembering what was revealed earlier.
Players work out a separate line of play for each hidden fact that could be true.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When part of the game is working out a hidden fact from clues, the secret itself gives players something to do.
pros: Players feel discovery as the answer is uncovered.
A fresh secret each game, as in Mastermind, lets the game be played again.
cons: Once a player knows the secret, there is usually little reason to play it again.
A fixed puzzle, like a crossword, is rarely repeated.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Learning how to play is itself hidden information, and the line between a secret and plain knowledge of the game is blurry.
pros: New players find interest in exploring what the game allows.
Players share the feeling of finding something out.
cons: Once the secret is known, the first interest does not come back.
The same knowledge, such as how to beat a boss, can count as a secret or as a skill, with no firm line between.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: With no hidden facts and no dice, as in chess and go, a player's reading of the board decides who wins.
pros: Players who like working out moves get a game that rewards it.
The game has a plain, open look that appeals to some players.
cons: Beginners and experts are far apart and cannot enjoy a game together.
Players feel pushed to calculate deeply to take part, and many leave.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Hidden cards and dice cut the reward for exact calculation, since the facts needed are not on the table.
pros: Beginners can keep up with experts without deep calculation.
Players spend less effort on counting and reading out moves.
cons: Players who enjoy exact reading-out have less to work with.
A loser can say the cards were against them.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Keeping track of which cards have been played is the main extra effort, and the first few things tracked give the most.
pros: Following one key card, such as the queen of spades in Hearts, gives a big return.
Experts can track more and gain a little each time.
cons: Tracking every card and who played it takes a lot of effort for a small extra gain.
A group that tracks cards pushes newer players to do the same.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: In a points game with open information, players near the end can add up the scores and work out exactly what each move gives.
pros: Players know where they stand.
The last choices are clear.
cons: At the end, players add up sums and judge little.
Players who enjoyed the looser early play may find the ending less to their taste.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Points kept secret, such as a hidden victory-point chit or hidden gold, stop players adding up everyone's total before a big move.
pros: Nobody has to count rivals' totals.
Money earned in secret, such as on a card kept hidden, lowers the reward for memorising totals.
cons: Players may try to memorise what others have earned.
Done badly, the tweak can make a dull task more irksome.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: A die roll or draw at the start of your turn means you cannot plan your move while others play.
pros: Drawing at the end of your turn lets a player plan during the wait, as in Scrabble.
A random element can still leave a turn easy to plan if its effect is small.
cons: Waiting feels longer when nothing can be planned.
An unlucky draw at the end of a turn can leave a player sad while they wait.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: With no dice, players can read out their moves while the other player thinks. Chess needs that waiting for moves of the same quality.
pros: Waiting time becomes thinking time.
Moves hold their quality without extra time on the clock.
cons: A beginner may find the wait long, since they cannot use it.
A skilled player may want even more time than the rules allow.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When players interact in pairs, the others wait while two of them settle things, as in the duels in Titan.
pros: The two players in the duel have a sharp moment of play.
Waiting players watch with interest, because the result affects them.
cons: Everyone else sits out for the length of the duel.
More players mean longer waits.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Where money or points are paid to you on other players' turns, as in Monopoly, waiting players watch every turn with interest.
pros: Other players' turns matter to everyone at the table.
Waiting is easier to bear when something can happen to you.
cons: The roll at the start of a turn leaves little to plan during the wait.
Rolling and moving along a track is routine work with few choices.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Real-time play with no turns removes waiting, but it asks for quick hands or clicks.
pros: Nobody waits for another player.
The game has a quick pace.
cons: Speed of hands decides more than planning.
Players have no time to rest, and fewer players can keep up.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: A clock on a thinking game makes it closer to a reflex game, the shorter the time the closer it comes.
pros: Shorter turns mean less waiting, as Starcraft trades downtime for needed skill.
Thinking games keep their thinking and add speed of thought.
cons: Slower players may be put off, as with Starcraft.
The shorter the clock, the more reflexes matter.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Secret choices made at the same moment work like a die roll nobody can see, as with penalty kicks in football.
pros: Each player has to guess what the other will do.
Players feel surprise when choices are shown.
cons: Each choice is private to its maker, so the other player can only guess.
The result is unknown to everyone until the reveal.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When an army or a base is hidden by fog of war, the game becomes a guess about where the other player is.
pros: Scouting gives players a task of their own.
Finding what was hidden brings a feeling of discovery.
cons: Players spend effort learning what the other player has done.
It is harder for onlookers to follow what is happening.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Poker is built on money, and is hard to play satisfactorily without it.
pros: A win paid in money may feel more real and more valuable.
The thrill of risk is part of what money gives.
cons: The game may feel empty once the money is taken away.
Poker players seldom treat points as if they were money.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: In gambling games the reward is often the dream of money and the thrill of risk. Most players do not expect to leave richer.
pros: Players get a thrill from risk.
Money can keep a game popular that would otherwise hold no interest.
cons: Most players lose money over time.
Without the stake the game can have little to hold anyone.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: In a game like a slot machine, nothing a player does changes the result, so there is no effort to put in.
pros: Anyone can play from the first minute.
The thrill of risk is a main reward of gambling games.
cons: Study and practice bring no gain.
A player cannot improve over time.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Rolling the die and moving along a track with no branches asks for no decision and has no skilful way to do it.
pros: Beginners can play at once.
The routine is rarely felt as a burden.
cons: Players have nothing to decide on a turn.
Skill has little to work on.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: A familiar fantasy world tells players what to expect: a dragon is more powerful than an ogre, and a card called Fireball suggests attack.
pros: Players guess what a card does from its name.
The rules take less time to learn.
cons: A new invented world gives players no such help.
Players may expect more from a card than its rules give.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: In poker there is much waiting, and some less skilled players stay in hands they might leave, to avoid sitting out.
pros: Waiting time can be spent watching opponents.
The pace gives time for talk.
cons: Players call in hands to end the wait.
Some players join several games at once to fill the time.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When players are knocked out in a real-time game, those who are less skilled sit out more, as in Counterstrike.
pros: All players who are still in act at the same time.
Real-time play has no waiting at all.
cons: Less skilled players sit out the most.
Sitting out makes it harder to improve.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When all the state is visible, as in chess, a viewer can see all of it, though that does not make it easy to understand.
pros: The whole position is directly visible to a viewer.
Arcade and split-screen games sidestep the problem of hidden information.
cons: Onlookers who know little may not see why a move is clever.
A complicated board can still be hard to follow.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: The more is hidden, the less a crowd can follow. Watching a game where hands are secret tends to feel less interesting.
pros: Players keep their secrets.
Showing the hands to the crowd can make the game more exciting to watch.
cons: Following one player's view is not what audiences tend to want.
Showing one player's cards to the crowd can annoy the other players.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: With one player moving at a time and everything in view, a broken rule is hard to hide while the other player is watching.
pros: Cheating is hard.
Both players can check every move.
cons: Players have to pay attention to each other's moves.
Simple mistakes show up quickly.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When play runs at its own pace and some cards are private, a broken rule is easier to hide because there is less chance to notice it.
pros: Play stays fast.
Secrets stay secret.
cons: Cheating becomes more practical when it is less likely to be detected.
Real-time pace gives opponents less chance to spot a broken rule.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Groups often play a changed version, for instance by giving money to whoever lands on a free square. Many do not know the change is not in the rule book.
pros: A group can fix a rule it dislikes.
The game keeps feeling new.
cons: Players may disagree about which version is the real one.
The game can turn into a different game.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When a game copies a real battle closely, the side that won in history may be almost certain to win again at the table.
pros: Players who like accuracy get what they want.
The side that lost can still try to last longer than expected.
cons: One side may have little hope of winning.
Players who want an even contest tend to leave.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: A story built on one or two heroes leaves few characters for many players. Someone may have to play a smaller part.
pros: Players act inside a story they know.
The story keeps a clear shape.
cons: Not everyone gets to be the hero.
A player who is not the hero may feel less important.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: One player who keeps adding places and people can keep a game running for months or years, with no fixed end.
pros: There is always something new to find.
Play can continue as long as the group wants.
cons: One person has to make new material all the time.
That person does more work than the others.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: A story with an ending gives players a natural place to stop. A game with no ending has no such place.
pros: A finished story feels complete.
Games with no explicit end tend to rest on varied play rather than content that runs out.
cons: Players often stop when the story ends.
Replaying a known story offers less to find out.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When scores are very fine-grained, players often pick their own cutoffs, such as one billion points at pinball or a marathon under four hours.
pros: Players aim at targets that matter to them.
Chunking a fine scale into coarser steps can make goals more compelling.
cons: Reaching the cutoff gives a natural moment to stop.
Players may care less about the exact score.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Without a rival to beat, players need other aims. They tend to set their own, such as a harder level or collecting everything.
pros: Each player picks a target that suits them.
Play lasts longer when goals keep being added.
cons: The designer has to supply goals that rivals would otherwise provide.
Once a player wins, later wins can feel too easy.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When both players choose in secret and reveal together, each tries to guess the other's choice. Picking at random, by a die, cannot be exploited.
pros: Neither player can see the other's choice first.
Guessing a rival's plan is the whole game.
cons: No single choice wins every time.
A player who is easy to read tends to lose.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: If each player may attack or give way, both attacking tends to hurt both. One attacking against a player who gives way tends to win everything.
pros: Players weigh whether to risk a fight.
Giving way can pay if the other gives way too.
cons: Each player wants the other to give way.
Two players who both attack can both lose more than if both had given way.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When each player gains points by taking more from a common pile, each has a reason to take extra, though everyone loses out if all do it.
pros: Each player can profit individually from the common pile.
The cost to everyone becomes clear as the pile shrinks.
cons: The cost of taking too much falls on everyone, not only on the taker.
The common pile may run out.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When two players need to pick the same thing at the same moment without talking, there may be two equally likely answers and no sign of which one.
pros: The game is a simple model of a coordination problem.
Players need to read each other.
cons: Both can pick different answers and miss each other.
Neither can tell which answer the other will choose.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When all moves are visible and one choice always beats another, players can cross off the beaten choices one by one.
pros: Players can work out what the choices lead to.
Many simple games can be solved by deleting weaker options one at a time.
cons: If only one choice is left, the game has nothing to decide.
If choices do not beat each other in turn, the game can collapse.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Talks, promises and penalties can change what a player gains from taking too much, so players may agree to take less.
pros: Players can agree limits on use.
Penalties can be set for those who break the deal.
cons: Agreements need someone to check them.
Players can break a promise when no one is looking.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: In a hearts-style game, taking every penalty card turns the lowest score into the highest, so a player far behind can gamble.
pros: A player behind has a way back.
The game can stay open until the last hand.
cons: A failed gamble leaves the player further behind.
Players ahead have to watch for one long shot.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: If the cards that cost points change from one deal to the next, players have to learn a new aim each round.
pros: Each deal feels like a new puzzle.
The same cards are worth different things at different times.
cons: Players need to remember which round they are in.
New players can lose track of what counts.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When players name how many tricks they will take, and need to hit that number exactly, a bid becomes a promise.
pros: Taking extra tricks can cost as much as taking too few.
Players weigh their hand against what the bid says.
cons: A bid that is only a little wrong still loses points.
Bidding adds a step before play starts.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When one side lays its partner's cards face up after bidding, the hidden information drops for that side.
pros: The side that won the bid knows all its own cards.
Elaborate bidding systems let partners tell each other about a hand while making it hard for opponents to bid well.
cons: Less hidden information means fewer surprises for the bidding side.
One player plays two hands, so the partners no longer sit equal.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: In poker, some cards are secret, some are public and some are shared, so a player reckons how much a rival's hand might hold.
pros: Each player knows something no one else knows.
Some cards are communal, so every player can use them in a final hand.
cons: Players act without knowing the full picture.
A player with few high cards can still stay in the hand.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Poker players call, raise or fold in turn during rounds of betting, and the book gives occasional bluffing as a rule of thumb so that rivals will call you when your hand is strong.
pros: Bets let players signal about cards nobody else can see.
A player can drop out at a cost.
cons: A big bet can scare a rival with the stronger hand.
Nerve counts as much as the cards held.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Moving round a board by dice, and asking questions about other players' cards when you arrive, mixes luck of movement with clue work.
pros: Rolling and moving along a track is busywork that players rarely find a burden.
Each place reached is a chance to ask about other players' cards.
cons: A solved puzzle seldom draws players back; once the secret is known, they move on.
Players waiting for the right room fall behind in the hunt.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When the aim is to bankrupt opponents, a board and dice decide where pieces land, and landing on rivals' property costs money.
pros: A player gains when rivals land on their property, and that happens on the rivals' turns, so watching stays interesting.
Players slowly drop out as money runs out.
cons: Money gives a leading player more power to make more, so a lead tends to snowball.
Players who are knocked out can end up waiting a long time.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: If teams advance only after a task is done, such as guessing a drawn word, each roll is earned by the whole team.
pros: Teammates share the work of earning each roll.
A whole team moves forward together.
cons: Teams that guess slowly seldom get a roll.
Players who draw poorly can hold the team back.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When players talk in an open period, then write orders in secret and reveal them together, promises can be kept or broken in one moment.
pros: Success is only possible through cooperation with other players.
Everyone learns who kept their word at the same time.
cons: Cooperation is expected to end in eventual betrayal.
A single betrayal can undo a long agreement.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: In a map game where nobody can take territory alone, players need others' support, and later those same partners may be attacked.
pros: Each player can choose whom to ally with.
Cooperation and betrayal both belong to the game.
cons: In Cosmic Encounter each turn's attack falls on a random opponent, so long-term alliances are hard to keep.
Trust built over many turns can end in one move.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When rules let several players share a win in different ways, deals can end with more than one winner.
pros: Several players can win at the same time, giving shared victories.
Alliances can end in a shared victory.
cons: Players may argue over how to split a win.
A partner may drop the deal when a solo win appears.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When teams are chosen in secret, one side tries to work out who the others are while those others hide.
pros: Every player has something to work out.
Talk and watching carry the game.
cons: A wrongly accused player can be removed early.
An eliminated player may go off and do something else.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: A moderator can keep the choices of one side private when each player's secret role needs to be known by someone.
pros: Secret decisions stay secret.
The moderator can also hold special powers for some players.
cons: One person does not get to play like the rest.
The game cannot start without that extra person.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: In Killer, a live game played over days or weeks, each player has a target to eliminate, a player who knocks someone out takes on that person's target, and the last player left wins.
pros: The game fits into ordinary days.
Players stay in the game while they are away from the table.
cons: The game can last longer than players want.
A player who is out has less fun than one still in.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When the group votes one player out each round, each player needs to win enough support from others to stay.
pros: Social standing counts as much as skill at tasks.
Players who are out can still affect the end.
cons: Voting can shut one player out for reasons outside the game.
Eliminated players may feel left out of the finish.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: A knocked-out player who cannot return watches the team carry on.
pros: Each player's choices matter to the team.
Short games keep the waiting short.
cons: Players out early can only watch.
A long game makes the wait harder.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When a group works together to keep one object in the air as long as possible, the only aim is to carry on.
pros: Everyone has the same aim.
Nobody is left out for being weaker.
cons: A slip by one player stops it for all.
The game can end suddenly and with no winner.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: In a race between two raindrops down a window, onlookers name the winner, and no player makes any choice.
