pros: Onlookers can join in at any moment.
Nobody needs to learn rules.
cons: Players have nothing to decide.
The result tells no one anything about skill.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: If players play as fast as they like onto shared piles, the first to run out of cards wins the hand.
pros: Both players act all the time.
Quick hands and quick eyes decide who gets ahead.
cons: Play with no waiting at all can be tiring.
Fast hands can count for more than thought, and most players cannot reach the click rates needed.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When one player makes a secret rule, the others learn it only by testing moves and hearing whether each was allowed.
pros: Each failed try tells the guessers something.
The rule-maker holds the knowledge in the game.
cons: The rule-maker can only answer yes or no.
The guessers may take a long time to find the rule.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Asking a named player for a card of one rank gives a player a reason to remember who holds what.
pros: Memory of earlier asks helps a player.
A player who asks for a rank has to hold one.
cons: A player who forgets asks without a plan.
The asker loses the turn after one wrong guess.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: If cards are matched in pairs and discarded, the one card without a partner decides who loses.
pros: Everyone but one player is safe at the end.
Matching pairs gives each draw some meaning.
cons: The loser is decided by where the odd card ends up.
Players who finish stop playing and only the possible losers stay in.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When the aim is to avoid being the last with cards, players choose when to play and when to keep.
pros: Players choose which cards to keep and which to play.
Different stages can use different rules.
cons: The game ends with only one loser, so others stop caring.
The last player holds cards for a long time.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: In a card game where a player may draw more cards, counting what is left and working out the odds can give a skilled player an edge.
pros: Played optimally, the game tends to favour the player.
The player still faces luck each hand.
cons: The edge can be hard to use in real play.
The house depends on players finding optimal play hard.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Rolling dice again, up to two more times, lets a player keep the dice that fit the combination they want.
pros: Players can soften some unlucky rolls.
Each throw gives a new decision.
cons: Choosing which dice to keep takes thought.
Some turns end with nothing useful.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: If items appear along the track that help players who are behind, a leader's lead can disappear.
pros: Players who are behind can make spectacular comebacks.
Players behind have something to hope for.
cons: Catch-up that is too strong takes away the cost of trailing, and players tend to find that frustrating.
Items add luck to a race.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When the aim is to empty your hand first and each play has to beat the one before, players choose when to hold high cards.
pros: Players decide when to hold cards back.
The last player to play leads the next round.
cons: Some seats start with an edge.
Those who do well in a hand move to the more favourable seats.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: In a game where the player can only lose in the end, the aim becomes a higher score than last time.
pros: Scores let a player compare today's play with last week's, or with another player's.
Each game is a new try at the same thing.
cons: There is no moment of winning.
The game always ends in a loss.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: Shapes fall faster and faster, a completely filled row disappears, and the game is lost once the grid fills to the top.
pros: Every drop asks for a quick choice.
Clearing rows keeps the game running.
cons: Time to think shrinks as play goes on.
The player can never win, and can only try for the highest score before losing.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When one player makes a hard shot and the next has to copy it, each throw sets a task for the others.
pros: Each player sets a challenge for the next.
Each throw is a task anyone can see.
cons: A hard shot can leave all others out of the game.
A player who misses collects a letter.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: If a player gets a letter for each missed shot and drops out when the word is spelt, players leave one by one.
pros: Skill at the shot decides who stays.
Players keep trying until the end.
cons: Players out early watch the rest.
A slip of the hand in one throw costs a letter.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When a teammate may only use gestures or drawing to get a word across, the rest of the team has to read the clue.
pros: Teams cheer each other on.
Players find new ways to say things.
cons: Clues can be misread.
A player who draws or acts unclearly can hold the team back.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: In the sandbox mode of a city-building game, players try different actions and watch what follows.
pros: Players learn by trying.
Nothing is lost by experiment.
cons: There is no score to tell a player how it went.
Players may lose interest without a goal.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When all moves can be seen but one exact move is right, a beginner cannot tell a helpful move from a useless one and plays like chance.
pros: An expert can play every game without a mistake.
Nothing is hidden.
cons: A beginner has no way to tell if a move helped.
Beginner and expert play very different games.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When players can offer to double the stakes mid-game, a leader's confidence is tested by the other player's answer.
pros: The leader can use the lead to press on.
The other player may leave and keep their loss small.
cons: Played without money, backgammon has less use for its doubling cube.
The money at risk changes how players think.

source.ref: Elias, G. S., Garfield, R. and Gutschera, K. R. (2012). Characteristics of games. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. ISBN 978-0-262-01713-8.

pairs.tendency: When players talk and make deals and then all give their orders at the same moment, alliances help the players in them while their allies keep their word, and fall apart when an ally betrays.
pros: In the experiments, negotiation raised the performance of bots in alliances when all the allies were trustworthy.
cons: Efficiency dropped sharply for a bot that was betrayed.

source.ref: Ferreira, A., Lopes Cardoso, H. and Reis, L. P. (2015). DipBlue: A Diplomacy Agent with Strategic and Trust Reasoning. Proceedings of the International Conference on Agents and Artificial Intelligence, 54–65. https://doi.org/10.5220/0005205400540065 (Pages cited are those of the open-access PDF.)

pairs.tendency: A bid made before a hand of tricks commits the bidder, and the hand shows whether the bid is kept. The cost of failing is known in advance.
pros: A bidder who makes more than the bid also scores the extra points
The bidder has a clear aim for the whole hand
cons: A failed bid can wipe out points won during the hand
If no one makes a bid, the seller has to pitch the trump himself

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When bids are made in points and scores count down to nothing, a bid that is made moves a player towards the finish and a failed bid moves them back.
pros: Every hand moves each player's distance from the end
Whoever brings his score to nothing first wins the game
cons: A sold bid moves the seller forward before any card is played
A failed hand throws away the points won in it

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When each player gets one bid in turn and the last speaker may sell or refuse, the order of speaking shapes the bids.
pros: Bidding goes round the table in turn, and every player gets a single bid
The last speaker hears every bid before choosing
cons: Early bidders have to bid without hearing the others
The last speaker may refuse every bid and keep the right

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When a player may beg after a low-card deal, the dealer chooses between giving a point and dealing new cards to both players.
pros: A low deal is not final
The dealer has a choice to make at every beg
cons: If the new trump turns out to be the first trump's suit again, the dealer has to keep dealing more cards until the suit changes
Each beg either costs a point or changes the hand for both players

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When points sit on cards that the trick winner collects, a player can send points to a chosen rival or away from a leader.
pros: Players with no hope of scoring can still shape who gains
A player who cannot make his points can still play them to the player whose score is lowest
cons: A player may spend a hand helping one rival instead of playing for themselves
The player in front can find points kept from them

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When the stock lies face up and each player refills their hand from it, only the cards in hand stay secret.
pros: After every trick each player is refilled to six cards until the stock is gone
The refill cards are dealt face up, starting from the winner of the trick
cons: The planning gain ends once the stock is used up
Players still have to guess what the other hand holds

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When a higher bid pays more and each missing trick costs more, players weigh how far to go before the hand starts.
pros: A cautious bid and a bold bid both stay open
A bold bid that succeeds pays more
cons: A failed bid costs more with each trick missed
A failed bid also doubles the pool

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In Boston, once a bid is made the other three players all play against the bidder, so the auction settles who stands against whom.
pros: Sides are settled by the bidding, with no secret roles
The three opponents share one clear aim
cons: One player faces three and carries the whole loss
A failed bidder pays each of the other players

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When a hand is scored on named cards rather than on the number of tricks, a few cards decide most of the hand.
pros: Players have several separate things to chase in one hand
A player with few tricks can still score
cons: One card can score several points at once
A deal can be played out with neither player holding a card that counts for game

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In Boston, a bid names how many tricks you will win, and any higher bid takes priority over a lower one.
pros: Players state their aim before a card is played
Riskier bids pay more, so the rules put a price on risk
cons: Other players can read part of your hand from what you bid
A bidder who falls short pays all three of the other players an amount that grows with the tricks missed

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When players share a row of face-up cards, each card played changes what the other can capture, with no direct attack.
pros: A move can protect a pile by building on it
Four cards lie face up on the table for both players to use
cons: The other player can take a build by holding the right card
A player who builds without holding the card to take it in lets his opponent take back the cards played since and play again

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When a hand scores for sets that add to fifteen, pairs and runs, choosing which cards to give away matters as much as choosing which to keep.
pros: Every discard helps one score and costs another
The dealer and the other player discard for opposite reasons
cons: Players learn many scoring combinations before a first hand
Counting a hand takes time and can start arguments over missed points

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When the aim is to empty your hand, each card you play also decides which suit or number the next player has to match.
pros: Whoever empties his hand first wins
A wild card gives a way out when you are stuck
cons: A player unable to match is left with two moves, a skipped turn or an Eight
With two players and the whole deck dealt, the game runs long

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When one player faces two allies, the lone player is given the right to swap cards, which evens up the sides.
pros: The smaller side gets extra power
Each hand has a clear lone player and two allies
cons: The lone player still plays against the combined cards of two people
Hands are thrown in when nobody wants to play alone

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When one player has to say whether to swap cards before the other, any pause shows how much the hand is worth.
pros: Quick decisions become part of the skill
A nondealer who plays on without proposing leaves the dealer no exchange either
cons: A slow thinker gives away information
Players need to learn the common hands by heart to decide fast

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When a turn shows cards that everyone sees, a failed turn gives the next player information the first player paid for.
pros: Each later player in turn tries to find a matching pair
The rules are short enough for a child to learn
cons: A player later in the order can use what earlier players showed
A player who finds a pair takes another turn, so one player can keep going

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When the cards that win tricks are not the cards that carry points, winning many tricks does not mean winning the hand.
pros: Players weigh winning a trick against which cards go with it
The last trick earns three points and also brings the discard pile
cons: Players learn two orders of cards
After the last trick both sides add up the points in their piles, and only the gap between the totals is reckoned

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When scores are marked on a track both players can see, the one behind takes more risks and the one ahead plays safe.
pros: The gap between players tells each how much risk to take
A player who is behind has a reason to try bold plays
cons: A player who is behind and pairs risks handing the other a pair royal
One lucky deal can close a gap that skill built

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When the side naming trumps scores for three tricks but gives the other side two points if it fails, hands with many high cards order up and the rest pass.
pros: Each hand starts with a small decision about how sure you are
A player with a weak hand may pass instead of ordering up
cons: A wrong guess hands the other side two points
A fourth trick adds nothing to the score of a hand with three

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When partners may not tell each other their hands, the cards they choose to play become their only way to share information.
pros: Partners learn to read each other's plays
When a player goes alone, his partner puts his hand face down and keeps quiet for the five tricks
cons: A card a player lets others know he holds can be called by the opponents
Partners who do not know each other's habits lose points

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: Every card played is seen, so a player can work out which suits others have run out of.
pros: Players use what they have seen to guess the hidden cards.
A very low card from a late player, with no Heart thrown on the trick, hints that he holds few cards of that suit
cons: Players have to remember every card that has gone.
A low card can also come from a long suit, so a reading from it can be wrong

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When players say before the first card how many tricks they will take, the highest bidder plays alone against everyone else together.
pros: Players weigh their own cards before they commit.
A wrong guess costs chips, so a bid carries weight.
cons: The table splits into one player and many.
A wrong bid is only found out once the cards are played.

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When two players play together, each can pass points into the other's tricks and keep points out of the other side's tricks.
pros: Partners can help each other with a high card or a low one.
An opponent usually answers his partner's lead and, when the partner plays third, leads a suit the partner lacks
cons: A remark made during play, by an active or a silent player, makes the offender hand the lone player ten points
Each counting card an opponent adds to a trick won by the lone player goes into the lone player's total

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In Skat's open bids the lone player lays their cards face up after the first trick. The opponents then see the whole hand.
pros: The opponents can plan every play.
Grand Ouverte outranks every other bid in Skat
cons: The lone player has no secret left.
A wrong guess about the first trick cannot be taken back.

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In Slobberhannes the aim is to avoid tricks: the first trick, the last trick and the trick holding the Queen of Clubs each add a point against whoever wins it, and the first player to reach ten points loses.
pros: A high card is a risk, so choices change round the table.
The other three players usually answer a lead with their lowest card of the suit, unless a win is certain
cons: Clubs Ace and King are hazardous to hold
A player who takes all three of those tricks in one hand makes Slobberhannes and scores one point more

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: A spare hand softens an unlucky deal. In Rounce, a player who dislikes their five cards may swap them for the unseen dummy hand.
pros: An unlucky deal can be changed.
Players still have a choice to make at the start.
cons: The dummy hand is unseen, so the swap is a gamble too.
The choice adds a step before the first card is led.

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In Sixty-Six the leader can close the stock before the cards run out and bet that the hand is already won.
pros: Closing stops all drawing, and the other player has to play on as the leader chooses
The hand has a clear moment of decision.
cons: A wrong guess gives the other player two points.
If the other player has won no trick yet, the cost rises to three points.

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When cards left in your hand lose points the moment another player goes out, holding back a set is a risk.
pros: Nothing extra is given for going out first, so rushing out earns no bonus
Points laid on the table cover the value of cards still held when another player goes out
cons: A finish by someone else turns held cards into lost points.
Laying down early shows others what you are collecting.

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When sets lie face up on the table, other players can add cards to them and take the points.
pros: A player who first notices a discarded card that fits a laid set can take it from the discard pile and score it
A set you laid down can help someone else.
cons: Laying a set down gives others a chance to use it.
A player who picks from the discard pile has to carry off all the cards in it

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In Go Fish each player in turn asks a single opponent for a rank, to build sets of four called books; an opponent holding that rank gives up every card of it, and otherwise the reply is go fish and the asker draws from the fish pile.
pros: A player whose request is met may ask again, of the same player or a different one
Remembering who asked for what becomes part of play.
cons: A refused request sends the asker to the fish pile, and the turn ends unless the card drawn is the one asked for
Players who forget earlier questions lose chances.

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In Go Fish you pick a player and take every card of a rank from them, so asking is a kind of taking.
pros: An opponent who holds the rank gives up every card of it
Players choose a target for their own reasons.
cons: The same player can be asked again and again.
A single refusal ends the asker's run of requests

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In Old Maid, pairs are thrown away until one card with no partner is left, and its holder loses.
pros: A player who completes a pair sets it aside and takes another pick
Nobody is out until the very end.
cons: The loser is simply the player left holding that card.
A card taken from another player's hand that makes no pair simply joins the taker's hand

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In Draw Poker, a player whose bet nobody matches takes the pool without showing the cards.
pros: A bluff can win without ever being found out.
When a bet is called, those left in turn their hands over, and the highest-ranking one takes the pool
cons: A player never learns whether the bluff was a bluff.
The cards alone no longer settle the result.

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In Draw Poker, players put in stakes and raise on the hand as first dealt, then each may draw from one to five cards, and a second round of betting follows once all hands are filled.
pros: A player can improve a hand they dislike.
A player may draw any number of cards from one to five, or keep the hand as dealt
cons: A player who stays in has to match each raise, or give up all that he has already put into the pool
The dealer goes round the table asking each player for the number of cards wanted, and betting resumes only after every hand is filled

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In Napoleon each player in turn bids how many tricks his hand will warrant or passes, and the highest bidder plays alone against the rest, who combine against him.
pros: Players judge their own hand before committing.
The other players team up to beat the bidder
cons: A bidder cannot check the guess until the cards are played.
A missed bid costs the bidder chips paid to each opponent.

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In Grabouche, partners may not speak about a play, and a word or gesture lets the other side place cards on the offender's pile.
pros: Partners learn to read each other from the cards they play.
The table stays quiet.
cons: A slip with a word or look costs the whole side.
A word or sign of praise brings the same penalty as one of complaint

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In Grabouche, a player can put a card on their own table pile, where opponents cannot use it, to block the other side.
pros: A player may stack table piles in descending order, or keep one pile all of one rank
Partners can use the cards on each other's piles.
cons: Playing to the middle can help the other side clear their pile.
Players need to keep a strict count of what lies on their own and their partners' table piles

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When a card can be bought before anyone has seen it, the price becomes a guess about what is hidden.
pros: When two players want a card, the one who offers most buys it
A card's worth is set by the players, not printed on it
cons: A buyer of an unseen card may pay for nothing
Where a Jack or Five costs a chip when turned up, the buyer of an unseen card pays it in place of the holder

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When the winning card is found by turning cards over, its holder may sell it instead of keeping the risk.
pros: Selling gives the holder a sure gain
The holder chooses between a price and a chance
cons: The seller may learn later that the card would have won
A buyer may pay for a card that is soon beaten

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In a partner game each player sits opposite a teammate, and the two win or lose tricks together.
pros: The two highest cutters partner each other against the two lowest
A lead can tell a partner what a player holds
cons: The same lead also tells the other team
A player with few high cards depends on the partner

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: The deal is random, but counting which high cards are still out lets a careful player make more of the same hand.
pros: Counting cards rewards close attention
After any low lead, the third player can locate exactly three higher cards in the leader's hand
cons: The second hand's choice depends mostly on how the first round's cards fall
To count the higher cards still out, a player takes the pips on the card fourth in rank away from eleven

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When the aim is to be first to win a set number of tricks, a hand can end with nobody reaching it.
pros: Three tricks in a single hand end the game for the one who takes them
Players can stop a leader by winning a trick themselves
cons: A hand with no winner leaves the prize on the table
Where a jink is allowed, a player who has won three tricks and plays on for all five but misses one scores nothing and cannot win on that deal

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When each player may name how many tricks they will aim for before play, the same hand can mean different games.
pros: Players pick a risk to suit their hand
Others hear the aim and can play against it
cons: A bold call can fail in front of everyone
Calling to lose every trick reverses the usual aim

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In Twenty-One a player examines his first two cards, which are dealt face down, and then asks for more one at a time, each dealt face up, going out of the hand on passing twenty-one.
pros: A player who is content says stay and lays his hand face down
Players who lose to the dealer toss their cards in unseen
cons: Going over twenty-one means the player busts and drops out of the hand
The dealer decides to stand or draw only after every player has stood, drawn or quit

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In a one-die game where you may throw again, the only choice is when to stop, and each throw may carry you over.
pros: The winner is whoever lands on twenty-one or nearest to it without passing it
The player decides after every throw whether to stop
cons: A player who stops early may be passed by a lucky thrower
A player cannot change what the die gives

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In dice poker a player may keep some dice and throw the rest again once, so a first throw that missed can be mended.
pros: Players choose which dice to keep
A second throw softens a first throw that missed
cons: Only one extra throw is allowed, so luck still leads
A kept pair can be lost when thrown again

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In a tile game where players draw from a stock and some tiles stay out of play, nobody knows exactly what the other holds.
pros: Players can guess from what is drawn and played
Leaving tiles unused keeps the guess open
cons: A player without a matching tile draws until one comes
A set where neither player can move is blocked, and the spots left in each hand are then counted

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: Each tile you lay changes which tiles the next player can use, so you shape their options without touching them.
pros: A player can block without any attack
The rules stay short
cons: A closed end can stall both players at once
A tile that is hard to place becomes a danger to hold

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In Mah Jong, hands are hidden but each discard is shown, so rivals can read which tiles a player is not collecting.
pros: Discards give out information for free
Players can estimate a rival's hand from what is thrown away
cons: A shown discard can help a rival finish a set
A player who settles on the same suit as the opponent on his left is unlikely to be given a chow or a pung by him

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When players pay each other the difference between their scores, someone who does not finish can still gain.
pros: Every hand counts, not only the finished one
A big hand can be worth more than finishing
cons: The player in the East Wind seat gets and gives twice the amount
Doubling rules can let one hand outweigh many

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When a wrong reply sends a player out, each call becomes a small test. In Simon Says, the leader's trick is to leave out the key words.
pros: One player is left at the end and wins
Players stay alert because a slip is final
cons: Early mistakes leave players waiting while others carry on
Simon may show a movement while leaving out the words, and players who copy it are out

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When one call is answered by the whole group together, every player's reply is on show at the same moment.
pros: One call tests every player at once
The leader can see who hesitates
cons: A player who obeys a command that did not come from Simon has to leave the game
A player who does not do what Simon says promptly has to leave

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When the reply to each call is a yes or no from one player, that player decides who moves and who stays.
pros: A player may carry out his task only after asking Mother's leave
Nobody can move without an answer
cons: A refusal from the Mother leaves the player in the same place
The Mother has to keep track of every player, and loses her position if she forgets where they are

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When a call has to be answered before a count of ten, the reply gets shorter and the pace stays high.
pros: Each catch is followed at once by a new name called and a throw back to the other side
When time is called the side with fewer players seated wins
cons: A player who throws wildly, or drops the bag sent to him, has to sit down
Hesitating counts the same as a wrong answer

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When the answer comes back in a disguised voice, the asking player works from the answers alone to find who spoke.
pros: Questions become the only tool for finding out
The answering player can change the voice to make it harder
cons: The player who is pointed at has to answer three questions from the blindfolded player
Only a correct guess brings a change of places

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In Hunt the Thimble the hider may guide the hunters with words running from warm to hot or cool to cold, or with music that rises as they near it, or may say nothing, but he may not mislead them.
pros: The hider can use spoken hints or music that rises as a hunter comes closer
Hunters can compare answers to track the object
cons: The hider may withhold his hints altogether, so a hunt can go on with no guidance
The hider may place the object in view, yet somewhere no one expects to look

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When a race is run through hops, kicks or throws, a single slip costs the turn, so the quickest player may not be in front.
pros: Boxes 4, 5, 7 and 8 call for a straddle, and every other box for a hop
Whoever completes the board first without faltering wins
cons: A stone in the wrong place, a landing on a line or a touch of the raised foot ends the player's turn
The same course feels different to players of different sizes

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When every dropped or missed object sends a player out, the circle shrinks and the pressure rises on those still in.
pros: Those left face the same task but fewer rivals
The game ends by itself when one player remains
cons: A dropped bag means the player has to step out of the circle
A single slip can end a long run

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When points depend on how near an object lands to a mark, a throw that misses the centre can still add to the score.
pros: A near miss still earns a few points
Smaller circles or a longer distance to the baseline make the game harder
cons: A bag in the inner circle is worth fifteen against ten in the second
The first group to reach 100 points takes the game

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When a turn goes on until the player slips, a skilled player acts for a long stretch while the others wait.
pros: Skill buys a longer turn
After a slip, the next player tosses the jacks again
cons: A missed catch of the ball, or a touch on a jack not being picked up, ends the turn
Turn length varies from player to player

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When a number needs three hits to close it, every throw has a purpose and each player keeps a small tally.
pros: A tally shows who is ahead on each number
Hits are marked in a column for each team, so progress on each number is visible
cons: Players need the score sheet to follow the game
A dart that bounces out is dead and is neither reshot nor scored, except in the opening shot at the bull's-eye

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In Numbers nobody wins or loses: the player who is hit takes the next throw and calls a new number, and play runs for an allotted period of time.
pros: Nobody feels they lost
A player hit is simply the next to throw
cons: Play stops only when the allotted time runs out, whoever has been hit
The thrower takes time to aim while everyone else stands still with backs turned

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When a player who is hit or caught joins the other side, the winning side grows as the other shrinks.
pros: Nobody sits out for long
The team that is ahead gains more throwers
cons: A losing side shrinks faster as it loses
Only the final B still standing counts as the winner

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When the actor may not speak and a clock runs, each turn becomes a quick race to be understood.
pros: The actor may show the whole idea or only some parts of it
A referee outside the game keeps time and sorts out disputes
cons: A hard idea can use the whole clock with no guess
An actor who freezes loses the turn to the other side

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In silent acting between teams, only the actor's own team guesses, so the team guesses together from one actor's movements.
pros: Teammates learn each other's signs
Rivals can enjoy the show without helping
cons: After the start a team may not talk, not even to settle what its agreed signs mean
A team that agrees signs early can pull ahead

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When the aim is for every player on a team to have had a turn, the race counts turns, not points.
pros: A correct guess passes the acting turn to a different member of the same team
Each player has a turn to be the actor
cons: A team stuck on one idea loses time for all
If a team runs out of time without a correct guess, the other team goes next

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: With no winner or loser in individual play, the acting and guessing become the whole point of the game.
pros: Nobody is out or left behind
Whoever guesses the idea is the next to act
cons: If time runs out with nobody guessing right, the next actor is the player seated left of the last
No spoken words, no spelling out of letters by sign and no props are allowed

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When one player knows the answer and a clock runs, that player picks which part of the idea to show first.
pros: The knower decides what to share
The clock stops long waiting
cons: The actor performs for his own team only
No word, no sign for a letter and no physical prop may be used to put the idea across

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When each answer starts with the last letter of the one before, and no answer can repeat, the pool of answers shrinks with every turn.
pros: A name already used may not be used again, so the choices run down
Players build on each other's words
cons: A repeat or a blank mind puts a player out
Players who are out wait until the game ends

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: A game that asks for a place name or a word from memory rewards what players already know, and shows what they do not.
pros: Players practise recall
Any group can set its own kind of answer
cons: A player who has no reference to offer, or says one already used, is out
Players have to hold in mind every reference already named

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When each wrong guess adds a part to a drawing, the guesser races to find the hidden word before the drawing is whole.
pros: The cost of a wrong guess is easy to see
Both players watch the same page
cons: The setter has no choices once the word is chosen
Wrong letters are written off to the side while the hangman is built up

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In a two-player guessing game, one player sets the puzzle and the other answers it, so each is working against the other.
pros: Each reply tells the other something new
After a correct guess the guesser becomes the one who thinks of the next word
cons: The setter is held to a real word that he knows the other player can spell
The guesser can only answer, not change the puzzle

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: In tick-tack-toe two players take turns placing X or O in a square, and the first to line up three of their symbols wins; the book prefers games between players of equal skill.
pros: The rules take a minute to learn
A line of three can run across, down or diagonally
cons: A game can end drawn when neither player gets a line of three
A player who sees the pattern early rarely loses

source.ref: Fitzsimmons, T. and Liflander, P. (1996). The everything games book: hundreds of classic games for all ages. Holbrook, MA: Adams Media. ISBN 978-1-55850-643-5.

pairs.tendency: When points come from the length of the diagonals each player builds, instead of counting tokens on the board, both players get nearly equal chances to fill the grid and the first-player advantage shrinks.
pros: Scoring patterns gives players more to plan than counting pieces.

cons: A bid built on hoped-for cards, not cards held, tends to fail.
A bidder who fails pays every other player.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: A bid counts the tricks a player can force, then leaves room for luck in a spare hand that others cannot see.
pros: A bidder can reckon an outside ace, or a king and queen together, as one trick.
The bidder can count on the spare hand adding a little.
cons: A bid that relies on one particular card in the spare hand tends to fail.
Each player has only one chance to bid, so bids have to be stretched to reach six or seven.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When partners share one score, one player's bid puts the points of the whole side at stake.
pros: Partners win points together when the bid is made.
Every player gets a say in the bidding before play.
cons: One partner's misjudged bid costs both of them points.
After a bidding mistake, the rules can bar the partner from bidding.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: A call that makes the other player doubt your hand can win the choice of trump without the cards to back it up.
pros: A hand with few high cards can sometimes push a rival into giving up the deal.
A schmeiss can be tried on a hand not strong enough for a sound take.
cons: The bluff can leave the caller making trump against a rival holding the top cards.
It works only when used rarely.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: A player who dislikes the proposed trump suit can pass the choice on, which softens an unhelpful deal.
pros: A player is not stuck with a first hand that does not suit.
The dealer gets a say in whether the cards are dealt again.
cons: Refusing means more cards are dealt and there is a new hand to judge.
A refused suit may come back and be thrown out again.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Watching which cards have been played shows which cards the others can no longer hold.
pros: The first plays in each suit show where a run of cards will stop.
If the 7 of Hearts was a first play, lower hearts led afterwards are sure to be stopped at the 6.
cons: The widow stays unseen by everyone but its buyer, unless the dealer takes it.
A player who cannot play has to draw cards until he can.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Once the face-down stock is gone, a player who followed earlier plays can work out the opponent's hand.
pros: The last tricks become a puzzle in which every card is accounted for.
Memory of earlier plays pays off in the final tricks.
cons: Counting every card is a heavy task, so many players track only trumps and aces.
Almost always the hand with more trumps takes the last trick.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When one player takes a contract and the other two play against that player, every trick becomes a contest between one and two.
pros: The two other players join in a temporary partnership against the contractor.
A contractor who is set loses the value of his bid from his score.
cons: The two opponents may not pass hints, so they work together only through the cards they play.
The contract holder is chosen by the bid, and the others cannot pick a different target.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When partners are fixed by who holds a called card, nobody is sure who is on their side until the cards fall.
pros: The partner shows up only as the cards fall during play.
The caller may end up playing alone without planning to.
cons: The holder of the called card has to stay silent, so friends cannot signal.
The caller starts the hand not knowing who will help.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When cards are added to a public layout from hidden hands, a player cannot tell whether the next card in the row is held by a rival.
pros: The layout shows everyone which cards open the way.
Sevens are always playable, and each one opens the eight and six of its suit.
cons: Choosing a card near the end of a row opens fewer plays for rivals.
A player stuck without a playable card has to pass and pay.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: A player can promise to take more tricks or points than needed for a bigger reward, and loses the reward if the promise fails.
pros: A bold promise can win much more than a safe one.
A maker playing alone scores 4 for winning all five tricks, against 2 with a partner.
cons: A failed promise pays the opponents.
A wrong claim of having won can cost the claimant points.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When tricks are worth nothing and only emptying the hand counts, a trick matters because of the cards it removes.
pros: Leading from the longest suit keeps cards of every suit for as long as possible.
The first player out wins at once, with no counting of points.
cons: A player who cannot follow suit has to pick up every card in the trick.
Taking up a trick sets a player back by several cards at once.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Two opponents team up against one contractor, yet each keeps a separate score for the tricks that player wins.
pros: Both opponents share the aim of defeating the contract.
Each still gains from winning tricks, so neither is only a helper.
cons: Every trick an opponent wins is worth 10 to him alone, whether or not the contract is made.
Neither opponent can see the other's hand, so help is guesswork.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Scoring for matched cards, such as a king and queen of one suit, sits beside scoring for tricks won.
pros: A hand can earn points before a single card is led.
A marriage, a king and queen of one suit, counts 40 in trumps and 20 in any other suit.
cons: Only one meld may be made in a turn, apart from the dix.
Rules about which matches may be counted at once grow long.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: A high trump is sold to the highest bidder while other cards are face down, so each price is a guess.
pros: Buyers pay for a chance, so each sale is a bet on what is hidden.
A player can buy up unturned cards to make sure of winning the pool.
cons: A buyer can pay a high price and still lose to a card not yet turned.
The price goes to the seller, not the pool, so sellers gain even when buyers lose.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When players choose how many chips to risk on one unseen card, counting the cards already seen changes the odds of each bet.
pros: A later bettor can strike out cards already shown and judge the odds more closely.
A bet can be anything from one chip to the whole pot, so one card can swing a lot.
cons: Every bet still rests on a single unseen card.
Keeping count of cards takes attention, and the odds often stay close to even.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Each player gives two cards to a crib owned by one player, so every deal is a choice between keeping points and denying them.
pros: The same cards are kept or given up differently depending on whose crib it is.
Players can lay away cards far apart in rank to starve an opponent's crib.
cons: The starter is turned up once the crib has been laid away, so the choice is made without it.
A player sometimes has to split a pair or a run to protect the crib.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When players add cards to one shared running total, each card played changes which scores the next player can make.
pros: A play can block a fifteen or a run before the other player reaches it.
Players read what the other might hold from the total on the table.
cons: There is no defence against a pair, so some scores cannot be stopped.
A player who says go while able to play has the cards he could have played counted dead, and the opponent pegs 2.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Face cards can only be taken by a matching card, so what a player holds in the last hand shows where the match is.
pros: A player who remembers the cards seen can work out what the opponent holds.
Keeping a card for the last play gives first chance at it next deal.
cons: Following every card takes a lot of memory and attention.
A card kept too long may be lost to a build the opponent makes.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: A player who lays a card on table cards to make a total keeps a card in hand that can take it.
pros: A build ties up a card in the hand, so the opponent can guess what the player holds.
A build can be increased or doubled, changing which card takes it.
cons: An opponent who holds the right card can capture the whole build.
A build that cannot be taken in costs the builder a point.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When players draw and discard to gather one suit and the lowest hand pays a chip, players drop out as chips run out.
pros: Players stay in until their chips are gone, and may play on once after that.
Knocking ends the hand early for a player who thinks the hand is high enough.
cons: Several players can share the lowest count and all pay at once.
A player who pays the last chip can be out on the next low hand.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Each player draws against the dealer and loses on passing 21, so the dealer's shown card guides how far each player risks.
pros: A player can stop at any time, so the risk is chosen.
The dealer's shown card gives something to judge each draw by.
cons: A player who goes over loses at once, even if the dealer later goes over too.
A dealer facing many players who stood may have to draw and go over.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When a player may swap a card with the neighbour, who has to accept, an unwanted card travels round the table.
pros: A turn is quick: look, keep or swap, then pass on.
Players holding a high card are pushed to hand it on.
cons: A player who is asked for a trade cannot refuse it.
In one version a king cannot be swapped, so its holder takes no part.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Cards in a row may only move onto a card of the same suit or rank, so the deal forces nearly every move.
pros: A game finishes in a few minutes.
One move can open up others, as moving a card onto a pile uncovers a further match.
cons: A player almost always loses, so winning is rare.
Reducing the number of piles is the only skill left.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When cards are built down in sequence and empty spaces let a player rearrange piles, skill can offset some luck.
pros: Empty spaces let a player plan and swap cards between piles.
Face-down cards turn up as piles are cleared, so a move can open more moves.
cons: A new row of cards cannot be dealt until every space is filled.
Moving a king into a space can use up the most useful space.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Players each have a pack and tableau and play onto shared ace piles at once, and the first to empty the reserve wins.
pros: Aces move to the centre when available, and every player may play on them.
Every player brings a pack and a tableau of his own.
cons: With no turns, players have to agree how to settle disputes.
Play can become disorderly if the rules of procedure are loose.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When two players build on their own piles and may place cards on the opponent's stock, getting rid of cards is also an attack.
pros: Placing a card on the opponent's pile clears the player's own pile.
Strict order of play settles who may do what and when.
cons: A player who breaks the order loses the turn.
The opponent's pile can be built on only in suit and sequence.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When the bank is sold by auction and all others may bet against it, the bid sets how much they can win or lose.
pros: The auction picks the player willing to carry the most risk.
Any player may cover part or all of the bank.
cons: A banker who loses passes the bank to another player.
The banker is never liable beyond the amount of the bank.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Players have private boards and a referee who only says no, check or capture, so they work out hidden pieces from the answers.
pros: An illegal try tells a player that a piece blocks the way.
A capture announcement tells where, but not what was taken.
cons: Someone has to act as referee and keep the true position on a third board.
The game needs three boards and two players kept apart.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When all bets are placed against a bank and a wheel decides each result, no betting system changes the result in the long run.
pros: Anyone near the table can join in.
Each bet has a stated payout, so the odds are open.
cons: Skill in choosing bets does not change the long-run outcome.
The bank keeps a fixed share of all bets in the long run.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When two partners sit opposite each other but one partner takes in all the cards, the partners mostly pool their scores.
pros: Scores from both partners are added together.
The pack runs out in three deals, and the dealer need not announce the last one.
cons: The play gives the partners little to do together.
One partner's play counts for the whole side.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Two players each play the same solitaire with their own pack and compare scores, so neither can affect the other's game.
pros: Each plays alone from a separate pack, and the scores are compared at the end.
Scores are easy to compare, and nine holes can be summed.
cons: Players cannot help or block each other.
A player's result depends only on their own pack and moves.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: With every mark in view and a row as the aim, the player who starts can force a win unless a rule limits them.
pros: The aim is plain and anyone can see it
The book calls it among the simplest versions of the Japanese game.
cons: The first player may hold a forced win
A smaller board or a limit on pieces is the way to keep it open

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: On a tiny grid with no luck, careful players tend to draw, so only beginners still win games.
pros: A smaller 8 by 8 board can be used, with twelve counters each.
On the small board, once all pieces are placed, play goes on by moving a piece to an adjacent empty square.
cons: Careful play on both sides tends to end level
Many players say the smaller board makes the game too easy.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: With nothing hidden and nothing rolled, practised players drew so often that organisers added a random start.
pros: The book calls it as deep as Chess in some respects.
Often the first player to crown a king wins the game.
cons: Practised players draw in many games
A chance opening had to be added to separate them

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: A rule letting players raise the stake gave Backgammon more room for skill on top of the dice.
pros: Choosing how to split a roll between pieces
Choosing when to double or give up
cons: A player whose roll will not let a stone enter from the bar loses the turn.
The stake can grow fast once doubling starts

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Sending an opponent's piece back to the start costs them turns, so one hit can swing a race.
pros: A hit stone goes to the bar and has to re-enter before its owner makes any other move.
A lone piece becomes a risk to leave out
cons: Each hit costs its owner one to four turns
A player far behind may hold pieces back to hit later

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Once you choose to roll again you have to claim more than your opponent did, so you cannot back out by calling the bluff.
pros: Rolling again can improve a low hand
A claim can be raised without showing the dice
cons: Rolling again closes the way to a challenge
Once his three rolls are used, a player either claims higher again or lifts the screen.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When the first to empty their hand wins, cheating early and telling the truth near the end tends to pay.
pros: Ranks that would fall late can be slipped into early plays as cheats.
A hand holding every rank is ideal for going out.
cons: The last cards are always doubted
A player short of a rank may have to doubt to fill their hand

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: A race to touch the same card needs a rule for whose hand was first, or every round turns into an argument.
pros: The first to slap a jack takes the common pile.
A player who has lost all his cards stays in until the next jack and returns if he slaps it first.
cons: Several hands land at once
Rules about the lowest hand, or the turning hand, have to settle ties

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When the shuffle decides everything, a game to win every card can run very long, and some groups never name a winner.
pros: The book offers it for filling idle time.
Children and adults play on equal terms
cons: No turn holds a real decision
The game can go on for a very long time

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: In Mill, a row of three lets you remove an enemy piece, so building and attacking are one move.
pros: One move builds and attacks together
Opening and closing a row can score again and again
cons: Forcing a row too early can leave your pieces locked in
Pieces already in a row cannot be taken

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Asking for a card tells everyone you hold one of that rank, so each question gives away a little.
pros: An asker keeps the turn while each player he names holds the card.
An asker is barred from naming a card he holds himself, so each ask points to a card he lacks.
cons: Every ask shows part of your own hand
Asking without holding a card of that rank costs a chip to each other player.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: A scorepad where each box is used once lets players put a low throw into a cheap box.
pros: Re-rolls soften a low throw
A spare box absorbs a failed try
cons: Each box is spent for the rest of the game
Late in the game few boxes are left to use

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When hits are told but not which shot made them, players have to work out where the ships lie while their own fleet shrinks.
pros: Only counts of hits are told
Each sunk ship cuts the shots left
cons: Losing ships also shrinks your own attack
The shooter calls out every square of his salvo, so the enemy learns where each shot fell.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: When points fall with every question asked, careful questions pay and wild guesses cost something.
pros: Each question has a price
Halving the choices is rewarded
cons: A subject nobody guesses scores only five for the answerer
After each question the questioner has to name a specific guess.

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: In a search where the only help is hot or cold, those who know can only say how near the seeker is.
pros: Everyone takes a turn as seeker
Hints tell more as the seeker nears
cons: The hint givers give away more as the seeker gets close
There is no result to compare afterwards

source.ref: Morehead, A. H. and Mott-Smith, G. (eds) (1983). Hoyle's rules of games: descriptions of indoor games of skill and chance, with advice on skillful play. 2nd revised edition. New York: Signet. ISBN 978-0-451-16309-7.

pairs.tendency: Seekers who spot the object sit down quietly and pretend to keep looking, so silence hides what you know.
pros: Sitting down says nothing aloud
Pretending to search hides your find
cons: A fixed stare gives you away
The last seeker is left looking alone

A second lie needs a lot of time and scratch paper

Cracking the code takes more guesses

A play using all seven tiles tends to come within a few turns
