cons: The first mover has a built-in edge
Opening moves tend to repeat

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When both players use the same stones to carry the ball home, a chain built for you also serves the other player.
pros: Delaying a jump to build a longer chain is a real plan
Jumped stones are removed, so a used chain is gone
cons: A chain can help the other player as much as you
Stones left a knight's move from the ball tend to be of little use

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In a race to line up five stones, the first player has an edge, so limits are put on his early moves.
pros: The rules are very short
Limits on the first player keep the sides close
cons: The first player still has an edge at the start
Extra limits add many rules to learn

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: A board that wraps round like a doughnut has no centre and no edge, so the first move has no favoured place.
pros: Lines can run off one edge and return on the other
Every starting point is alike
cons: Players find it hard to picture a line that leaves one edge and comes back
A flat sheet of paper needs a rule for the wrap

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When any of several shapes wins, one stone can threaten more than one, and a threat to close a ring gains time.
pros: Many ways to threaten, with one simple rule
Draws are very rare
cons: A ring is almost never completed, so it works mostly as a threat
Three winning shapes are more to learn than one

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Scoring each word at double the one before it, 10, 20, then 40, makes one long word worth as much as several short ones.
pros: A line such as SCATS scores the same as one word or as two overlapping ones
Overlapping words score separately
cons: Only the longer word counts when one word sits inside another
A score table is needed

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When every player writes the same called letters into a hidden grid, everyone builds with the same pieces but ends with a different pattern.
pros: Little equipment is needed
Each player's grid is their own plan
cons: Nobody sees how others did until the end
More players means less room for strategy

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Winning by capturing a run of numbered pieces, such as 4-5-6-7-8, makes players choose which pieces to take, not only how many.
pros: Leaving the opponent with no legal move is a second way to win
A win comes from capturing five pieces whose numbers form a run
cons: Players have to track the numbers taken and left
Taking any piece is not enough to win

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Anyone may call a word the moment they see it and others may steal it, so no word is safe.
pros: Nobody waits for a turn
Stealing one's own word is allowed, which lengthens it and makes it harder to take
cons: A word you have made is not secure, since other players may steal it
Players need to agree in advance which words count

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When every move has to flip at least one piece, taking fewer pieces early tends to leave the other player with fewer moves.
pros: Holding back leaves the other player short of choices
Key squares such as corners fall late in the game
cons: Taking many pieces early tends to give the other player more moves
Players are drawn to the move that takes the most pieces

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: If captured pieces change colour instead of leaving the board, a lead can turn round in a single move.
pros: A captured piece changes colour and can be moved by its new owner
A player who is behind can come back in one move
cons: A wall of pieces can look safe and still be open to a recapture
Without extra rules a player can build an unbreakable fortress and force a draw

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When a player can still take points already stored away, a lead is not final until the game ends.
pros: The result stays open to the end
A player who is behind keeps a chance
cons: Points kept in a store are never completely safe
A player cannot count on a lead

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When the player sowing beads may choose which bead goes into which pit, the moves per turn rise from a handful to hundreds.
pros: The order of sowing matters
The same rules suit longer and shorter boards, and the 2x3 game is far from trivial
cons: A player has far more moves to weigh each turn
Beads of several values have to be kept straight

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Moving a marker along a track instead of placing a stone turns a pass into points and evens out the first move.
pros: Passing brings the marker a space nearer to the one who passed
The first-move edge can be adjusted by where the marker starts
cons: A separate track has to be drawn
Players have to learn to add the marker points

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: With fewer shelters than pieces, players race to fill them and can shut each other out, and the one left outside loses.
pros: Only one piece has to find a place
Filling a shelter can block another player
cons: One slow piece decides the whole game
A large board and many pieces take a long time

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: If both teams can score in the same game, players play a series until one side reaches an agreed total.
pros: A captured raja does not end the game, since its immobile army can return to life
There are several ways to score
cons: A series takes more time
Players have to keep a running tally

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When dice only say which kind of piece may move, and a player may use one die, both or neither, luck limits choices.
pros: Allies may talk over the roll
A player can skip a roll that does not help
cons: A lucky double can hurt the other side heavily
Four players take a long time over one game

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Without dice, allied armies play pure strategy, and the order in which allies and rivals move matters as much as each piece.
pros: Every move comes from a player's choice
Allies can plan together
cons: Players have to keep track of the turn order
A mistake in order cannot be blamed on a roll

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: The dealer knows the secret rule and, once play begins, may only say right or wrong, so everyone gets the same plain answers.
pros: The dealer cannot steer play
The rule is written down to be checked afterwards
cons: One player sits out each round as dealer
Dealers usually score higher than the average, so a player who never dealt gets 10 points added

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Players test guesses about a hidden rule by seeing which plays are accepted, much as scientists test guesses about nature.
pros: Every play gives the whole table a clue
A wrong play still gives information
cons: A wrong play costs cards
Beginners tend to set a rule harder than they think

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When the dealer's score depends on the others' scores, a secret rule neither too easy nor too hard pays the dealer most.
pros: The dealer has a reason to set a fair puzzle
Players test guesses about the secret rule, as scientists test ideas about nature
cons: Scoring takes several steps to work out
A rule that lets half the cards be played is harder to find than one that lets a quarter be played

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In charades with bidding, players bid how few minutes and seconds they need to get a teammate to name the phrase.
pros: A bid is a time, such as two minutes, that the player expects to succeed within
The clock gives a clear pass or fail
cons: A bold bid that runs out of time loses the team a point
The game needs a trustworthy timer

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: The team of the lowest bidder earns a point if a teammate names the phrase within the bid, and loses a point if not.
pros: Teammates share the reward for a quick guess
Any number of teams can take part
cons: One player's boast can cost every teammate a point
Each team needs a bidder who can judge how hard a phrase is

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Before bidding, one player from each team sees the secret phrase. They then bid on how fast they could act it out.
pros: Bidders bid with the answer in front of them
Both bidders see the same phrase, so bids compare judgement
cons: The actor can only mime, so a low bid is hard to keep
A low bid tells rival bidders the phrase looks easy

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Haggle each player gets a sealed envelope of twelve cards and trades with anyone, for cards or for information.
pros: Deals can be made any way: card for card, information for information
Nobody can tell which suit to chase
cons: Each information sheet gives only some of the information about what cards are worth
A player judges every deal knowing only part of what the others hold

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Haggle each scoring rule sits on a secret sheet, so players piece together how cards score by trading sheets.
pros: Trading information matters as much as trading cards
Two sheets read together tell more than either alone
cons: The host has to write rules that do not contradict one another
A player may trade away a sheet that was worth a lot

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Haggle all trading ends before the host scores each envelope, so nobody knows the totals until the end.
pros: Trading stays lively because players cannot easily tell which suits to collect
The final choice of which cards to hand in decides the result
cons: The host needs time to score every envelope by hand
Turning in over 15 cards means the extra ones are dropped at random before scoring

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Haggle the first twelve cards are dealt by chance, but trading lets a player swap away cards they do not want.
pros: Trading softens a first hand with little use
Caps on the highest cards stop a lucky deal from deciding the winner
cons: Players who are dealt useful information sheets still start ahead
The host has to design the caps with care

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Super Babel players trade cards one for one to build two five-card poker hands, or one special ten-card hand.
pros: Equal trades keep every hand at ten cards
Players can call out what they need or keep their hands secret, and alliances can form
cons: A scorekeeper has to record every hand and reshuffle
Players need a time limit agreed beforehand

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Super Babel has no turns. Everyone trades at once until a set time, such as twenty minutes, ends the game.
pros: Players bargain whenever they like
A player who goes out gets a new packet and rejoins at once
cons: The game is made for fifteen or more players, so small groups have few partners
A non-playing scorekeeper is needed

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: A doubling cube lets a player double the stakes of a dice game. The other accepts, or gives up the game.
pros: Judging your own winning chances becomes a skill that decides a series
The same cube suits other race games, such as Parcheesi
cons: Judging the odds is hard, and the score of a match changes the choice
Refusing a double loses the game at once

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Moultezim and Gioul pieces cannot hit a single enemy piece, and in Plakato a hit piece is pinned instead of sent off.
pros: Progress is never sent back to the start
Plakato and Moultezim play as in backgammon apart from the listed changes
cons: A pinned piece cannot move until the hitting piece moves away
Players lose the sudden swing of sending a piece home

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Dice Chess a die decides which kind of piece may move, but every piece stays in view.
pros: Strong players, even grandmasters, play it for light relaxation
Some players let a player pass when a legal move exists but is not wanted
cons: Cheap dice may not be weighted accurately, so a 6 can come up far more often than a 1
A roll for a missing or blocked piece is thrown again

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Refusal Chess a player may reject the opponent's move, and in Compromise Chess the opponent picks one of two offered moves.
pros: The ideas of refusing and of offering two moves can be added to nearly any strategy game for two
Tactics and psychology both matter
cons: Players slow down to weigh what to offer
A single legal move cannot be refused

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Crash each player guesses a hidden five-letter word, and the other reports how many letters sit in the right place.
pros: Early salvos of several words give a player several scores at once
The game needs only paper and a dictionary, so letters can carry it
cons: A wrong score from the replier loses the game
Both players need to agree on a dictionary first

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Double Move Chess gives each player two moves a turn and drops check, so games tend to end quickly.
pros: Short games finish in fewer letters
Each letter carries two moves
cons: Check and checkmate are dropped, so the king needs watching on every move
Moving into check is allowed, which changes habits learned from ordinary chess

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In map-colouring games players colour one region a turn, and the first player with no legal region to colour loses.
pros: Players block each other only through the colours already placed
Extra colours make the game harder to work out
cons: Giving each player their own colour makes it harder still
Touching regions can end the game suddenly

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Finger Baseball both players show one to five fingers at the same moment, and a match gives the batter a hit.
pros: The game needs no equipment beyond one hand
Hidden choices stop a fixed habit from working for long
cons: An observant opponent can use any pattern in your choices
No single choice wins every time

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Ghost each player adds a letter. A rival may challenge a letter they think leads to no word, and the speaker then names a word.
pros: A bluff is tested at once by the challenge
The game needs no equipment
cons: A wrong challenge costs the challenger a letter
Adding letters at either end, as in Super Ghost, makes the possibilities very hard to count

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Kickball Golf each player kicks a ball at a tree or can, hole by hole, against a fixed par.
pros: One player can play alone against par
Each round takes only a few minutes
cons: A ball in the way needs marking with a leaf or twig
Kicking needs open ground clear of windows and children

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Poison croquet a ball that finishes the course turns poison. It knocks out any ball it hits.
pros: Finishing does not end the game for the finisher
Finished players stay in the game and threaten others
cons: A poison ball that hits the stake is out
Knocked-out players wait while the game goes on

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Nim a counting rule shows the mover which objects to take, so a player who knows it wins from many positions.
pros: The rules and equipment are very simple
Adding a second dimension of rows and columns makes the game hard again
cons: Once the rule is known, winning becomes routine
Two equal sections let the second player copy every move

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: When each player gets a few re-throws, or coins to nudge a roll up or down by one, an unwanted roll can be answered.
pros: A player can plan when to spend a re-throw.
Rethrows can be traded for properties or bought for cash in Monopoly
cons: Players have to keep count of what they have left.
Keeping rethrows to four or five makes the choice of when to use them harder

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: With a list of all 36 rolls to cross off, and no reuse until the list ends, luck drops out of the dice.
pros: Winning depends on the order in which rolls are used.
Nobody wins by throwing more double sixes.
cons: The game stops feeling like a dice game.
Each player keeps a list and crosses off rolls.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: With the list of unused rolls open, the chance of any roll is either certain or none, and both players can see which.
pros: Each player can see which rolls the other has left.
Counting replaces guessing at odds.
cons: Using up every roll that holds one number gives the other player a fixed target.
The game becomes a very different one, which the book names as the drawback

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In a game by post, players can take the next dice roll from a public number they agree on, such as a temperature.
pros: Both players can check each roll against the same published number.
No third person is needed to throw the dice.
cons: The source of numbers has to be agreed before play.
Each roll waits until the number is published.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In a game by post, each move goes on a card or letter, written in a short, clear notation.
pros: Players can think as long as they like about a move.
People who live far apart can play.
cons: Using a referee to roll the dice brings delay and extra postage
The two players need an agreed way of writing moves.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Giving one player more re-throws than the other can offset the edge of going first.
pros: The edge of moving first can be reduced by a small gift.
The same gift can serve as a handicap between players of unequal skill
cons: Both players need to keep count of the rethrow options they have left
A player with fewer re-throws has less to fall back on after an unwanted roll.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: If players throw three dice and choose which two to use, each throw still leaves room for a choice.
pros: Players decide which numbers to keep.
More choices give a player more chance to control the outcome and show skill
cons: A change that seems promising can have unwanted consequences that are hard to foresee
Moves become less of a surprise.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In a game of pure skill, if sitting back and waiting is the winning plan, both players wait for the other to weaken.
pros: A reward for attacking, such as a promotion, gives players a reason to move forward.
More mobile pieces give attackers more ways in.
cons: Games can run long and may never end.
A player who attacks can open weaknesses in their own position.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: Giving each player two moves a turn instead of one can raise a player's attacking power and shorten the game.
pros: Attacks come faster.
The game can end sooner.
cons: The other player waits through two moves before replying.
A plan can be finished before the other player can answer.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: If a game seems to favour one side, players can bid for the right to go first.
pros: The player who values going first most pays for it.
Both players start with a say in who moves first.
cons: A fully even balance is impossible when forces are unequal and draws cannot happen
Players need some way to measure what going first is worth.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: If no player may recreate an earlier board position, players have to vary their moves instead of repeating them.
pros: Fewer games end in a draw by repeating moves.
A player who is blocked can make a threat elsewhere first, then come back.
cons: A player has to vary the position and may not repeat it even once
A fight over one spot can last many turns, until one player runs out of threats.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In a Refusal game, the other player may reject a move, and the mover then has to make a different one.
pros: The other player shapes which moves are played.
The game is challenging psychologically as well as tactically
cons: A player can be pushed into a move they did not first choose.
Each turn takes longer.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In a Compromise game, a player proposes two moves each turn and the other player picks which one is played.
pros: The other player has a hand in every move.
The idea can be added to nearly any strategy game for two
cons: Each turn needs two usable ideas instead of one.
The strongest move may never be on the table.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Open Scrabble, all tiles lie face up in one line and players draw only from its two ends.
pros: Each player can see exactly what the other can take.
Luck leaves the tile draw.
cons: Working out what the other will be able to take is very hard.
Racks have to stay in view all game.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: In Double Bughouse, two teams play on two boards with a clock each, and a piece one partner captures goes to the other.
pros: Partners can talk and ask each other for a piece.
A team can win when an opponent's clock runs out.
cons: A player in trouble may stop moving and let the clock run, hoping a partner wins first.
Play gets noisy and rushed.

source.ref: Schmittberger, R. W. (1992). New rules for classic games. New York: John Wiley & Sons. ISBN 978-0-471-53621-5.

pairs.tendency: On a sacred board the squares carry meanings, so a step up a ladder or down a snake is also a small lesson about a virtue or a vice.
pros: Each ascent or descent invites the player to reflect on their own actions

source.ref: Sharma, M. (2025). From Moksha to Milton Bradley: The Historical Journey of Snakes and Ladders. SocioHumania: Journal of Social Humanities Studies, 2(1), 25–35. https://doi.org/10.70063/sociohumania.v2i1.90

pairs.tendency: A ladder-and-snake board can carry present-day concerns, with snakes standing for things like deforestation or corruption and ladders for things like recycling or schooling.
pros: The same simple format can be re-dressed for a local issue

source.ref: Sharma, M. (2025). From Moksha to Milton Bradley: The Historical Journey of Snakes and Ladders. SocioHumania: Journal of Social Humanities Studies, 2(1), 25–35. https://doi.org/10.70063/sociohumania.v2i1.90

pairs.tendency: In a game where everyone is on one team, hiding each player's cards makes it harder for one dominant player to run the group's decisions.
pros: Each player has to take part and talk the choices through.

source.ref: Sillaots, M. (2026). MitiGate: Risk Management Collaborative Tabletop Strategy Game. European Conference on Games Based Learning, 20(2), 747–755. https://doi.org/10.34190/ecgbl.20.2.5326

pairs.tendency: In a team game that is lost if any objective falls too far, cards that soften a die roll's damage make the game easier to win when they are balanced against the risks.
pros: Players accepted the uncertainty of the roll as part of the problem.
cons: The game became less punitive and easier to win.

pairs.tendency: In Cribbage, each player chooses which two cards to give away, knowing the rest are meant to make sums of fifteen, pairs and runs.
pros: After looking at the cards, each player puts two aside to form the crib
Many small patterns can score at once
cons: A hand is hard to count for a beginner
The crib gives the dealer extra points from cards both players helped pick

pairs.tendency: In Blackjack, the dealer keeps one card face down while players keep asking for more cards, each one a risk of going over 21.
pros: A player decides how much risk to take
The hidden card keeps the dealer's total unknown
cons: A player who goes over loses at once
The dealer wins ties, which tilts the game

pairs.tendency: In Euchre, the player who names trump may play alone, trusting one hand to win all five tricks for double points.
pros: Playing alone pays more if it works
The choice is the player's own, made from the cards in hand
cons: A lone hand leaves the partner out of the round
If the plan fails, the other side scores

pairs.tendency: In Bridge, one partner lays all their cards face up as the dummy, and the other partner plays both hands.
pros: The team plays with all its cards in view to one player
The opposing side sees one hand it can plan against
cons: One player does all the choosing for the team
The dummy hand goes down only after the opening lead

pairs.tendency: In Whist, partners sit facing each other against the other two, without any bidding or dummy, and the side that wins more than six tricks scores a point for each extra trick.
pros: The two highest cards drawn make one partnership
Won tricks are stacked overlapping so everyone can see the tally at a glance
cons: Only tricks beyond the first six score
A team has to win two of three games to take the rubber

pairs.tendency: When you can only ask for what you already hold, each question shows other players part of your hand.
pros: Players learn to remember who asked for what.
Even young players can follow the rules.
cons: A player may ask only for a rank she already holds
If the stock runs out, the most books wins

pairs.tendency: Everyone pairs cards off and throws them away. The single unmatched card decides who loses, and nobody wins.
pros: Players discard any pairs they hold at the start
A player fans out cards facedown to the neighbour on the left, who takes one
cons: The game has no winner, only a loser who is left with the odd queen
Play runs until every player has paired and discarded

pairs.tendency: Cards are turned over one pair at a time, so each player sees where cards sit and has to remember it.
pros: A player who finds a match removes the pair and goes again
One person can play it alone as practice
cons: A pair that does not match is turned back facedown and the turn passes on
Play goes on until every card is gone from the table

pairs.tendency: In rummy the first to empty their hand wins, so players get rid of high-value cards first in case someone else goes out.
pros: A turn starts by taking a card from either the stock or the discard pile
A player can lay off cards on melds already down, whether they are his own or an opponent's
cons: Players holding high cards late lose many points.
A player who lays every card down as melds in a single turn collects double

pairs.tendency: In Crazy Eights a player may keep a wild card back for the end, or draw extra cards to have more choices.
pros: A player may keep drawing from the stack at any turn, even holding a playable card
Holding more cards sometimes gives more options.
cons: A player with an eight left when another wins loses many points.
A sudden end can leave a planner holding a wild card.

pairs.tendency: In Spit both players move at once and the hand ends in seconds. Quick eyes and hands decide who clears their cards first.
pros: Rounds are very short.
Players are always busy, with nobody waiting.
cons: Only one hand may be used, and only one card moved at a time
Each card played has to be one step up or one step down from the card it covers

pros: Players turn cards up one at a time until a jack appears
The first player to cover the pile with a hand takes it all
cons: The game runs until one player holds every card
Tied slaps need a rule to settle them.

pairs.tendency: In I Doubt It a player lays down cards while saying what they are, and plans which cards to play and when to tell the truth.
pros: Players plan the order of play.
A challenge early in the game lets a player fill gaps in their hand.
cons: A player can end up with many cards from one wrong challenge.
A player wins by putting down a last card that goes undoubted or proves true

pairs.tendency: Each player sees only their own cards, so the leader plays without knowing who can follow suit or trump.
pros: Every trick holds a small surprise.
Remembering played cards pays off.
cons: An uneven deal limits what a player can do.
Players who track every card may take longer on each play.

pairs.tendency: In poker each bet, call or raise can be a bluff, so players decide how much to risk on a hand others cannot see.
pros: Betting limits keep risk small.
Folding lets a player stop losing.
cons: A big bet can win a pot with a low-ranked hand.
Players who bluff often lose chips fast.
